cases.title: Novartis AG v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Novartis AG, a Swiss pharmaceutical giant, filed a patent application in
India for the beta crystalline form of Imatinib Mesylate, a life-saving
drug used to treat chronic myeloid leukemia (marketed as Glivec). The
drug was a derivative of a known substance (Imatinib). The Indian Patent
Office rejected the application, citing Section 3(d) of the Patents Act,
1970, which prohibits the patenting of a new form of a known substance
unless it results in a significant enhancement of known efficacy.
Novartis challenged the rejection, taking the matter through the Madras
High Court, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB), and
ultimately to the Supreme Court of India.
cases.issues:
Does the beta crystalline form of Imatinib Mesylate qualify as an
"invention" under Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act?

What is the precise legal interpretation of "efficacy" under Section 3(d)
of the Patents Act regarding pharmaceutical derivatives?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Novartis AG)
Novartis argued that the beta crystalline form was completely new, non-
obvious, and had industrial application. Regarding Section 3(d), they
contended that "efficacy" should be interpreted broadly to include
enhanced physical properties, such as thermodynamic stability and
improved flow properties, which made the drug easier to store and
manufacture.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Union of India / Generic Manufacturers)
The respondents argued that Section 3(d) was specifically designed to
prevent "evergreening"-the practice of extending patent monopolies by
making minor, non-therapeutic changes to existing drugs. They argued that
for a pharmaceutical compound, "efficacy" must strictly mean "therapeutic
efficacy" (the drug's ability to cure disease), which the new form did
not significantly enhance.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the Union of India,
dismissing Novartis's appeal and denying the patent for Glivec.
cases.reasoning:
The Court conducted a rigorous analysis of the legislative intent behind
India's patent regime, particularly following the TRIPS agreement. The
Court held that Section 3(d) sets a higher threshold for patentability
for derivatives of known substances. The Court strictly defined
"efficacy" in the context of pharmaceuticals as "therapeutic efficacy."
While the beta crystalline form showed improved physical properties
(stability, hygroscopicity), Novartis failed to provide empirical data
proving a significant enhancement in the drug's therapeutic effect on
patients compared to the known base substance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Prevention of Evergreening: The Supreme Court firmly established Section
3(d) as a robust safeguard against the evergreening of pharmaceutical
patents.

Standard of Efficacy: In pharmaceutical patents, mere discovery of a new
form with enhanced physical properties is insufficient; the applicant
must demonstrate a significant enhancement in therapeutic efficacy.

cases.title: Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak
cases.facts:
Eastern Book Company (EBC) publishes "Supreme Court Cases" (SCC), a
highly regarded law report in India. EBC obtains raw, unedited judgments
from the Supreme Court, to which they add headnotes, cross-references,
paragraph numbering, and formatting. D.B. Modak and others launched
software containing the text of Supreme Court judgments, directly copying
the paragraph numbering and structural formatting created by EBC. EBC
sued for copyright infringement, claiming their edited versions of the
judgments were "original literary works."
cases.issues:
Can copyright subsist in court judgments, which are public documents?

What is the standard of "originality" required under the Indian Copyright
Act, 1957, to protect derivative/edited works?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Eastern Book Company)
EBC argued that while the raw judgment is public, the extensive editorial
labor, skill, and capital invested in copy-editing, adding paragraph
numbers, and creating cross-references transform the raw text into an
original literary work, protected under the "sweat of the brow" doctrine.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (D.B. Modak)
The respondents argued that judgments are government works and belong in
the public domain. Adding mere paragraph numbers and correcting
typographical errors are trivial, mechanical acts that lack the necessary
creativity to warrant copyright protection.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled partially in favor of EBC, establishing
a new standard for originality, but denied copyright in mere copy-
editing.
cases.reasoning:
The Court rejected both the British "Sweat of the Brow" doctrine (which
grants copyright for mere labor/investment) and the strict US "Modicum of
Creativity" doctrine (from Feist Publications). Instead, the Supreme
Court adopted a middle path: the "Skill and Judgment" test (borrowed from
Canadian jurisprudence). The Court held that to claim copyright in a
derivative work, the author must expend skill and judgment that involves
some minimal degree of creativity, not merely mechanical labor. The Court
ruled that EBC's paragraph numbering and copy-editing were mechanical and
not copyrightable. However, EBC's creation of headnotes and selection of
specific cross-references required legal skill and judgment, and thus
enjoyed copyright protection.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The "Skill and Judgment" Doctrine: India's defining standard for
copyright originality. A work must originate from the author and involve
a minimal degree of creative skill and judgment, sitting between pure
labor and high creativity.

Public Domain Derivatives: Merely formatting or correcting public domain
documents does not create a new copyrightable work.

cases.title: Bayer Corporation v. Natco Pharma Ltd.
cases.facts:
Bayer Corporation held the Indian patent for Sorafenib Tosylate (marketed
as Nexavar), a life-extending drug for kidney and liver cancer. Bayer
priced the drug at approximately ₹2.8 lakhs for a one-month supply,
making it unaffordable for the vast majority of Indian patients. Natco
Pharma, an Indian generic manufacturer, applied to the Controller of
Patents for a Compulsory License under Section 84 of the Patents Act,
proposing to sell a generic version at ₹8,800 per month.
cases.issues:
Were the statutory conditions for granting a Compulsory License under
Section 84 of the Patents Act satisfied?

Does pricing a life-saving drug beyond the reach of the general public
mean the reasonable requirements of the public have not been met?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Bayer Corporation)
Bayer argued that it had invested billions in R&D and needed to recoup
costs. They argued that "reasonably affordable price" should factor in
the cost of innovation. Furthermore, they had a patient assistance
program providing the drug free to some patients, arguing they were
meeting the public's requirements.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Natco Pharma)
Natco argued that all three conditions of Section 84 were met: (1) the
reasonable requirements of the public were not satisfied because only a
fraction of patients received the drug; (2) the drug was not available at
a reasonably affordable price; and (3) the patented invention was not
"worked" in the territory of India (Bayer was merely importing it, not
manufacturing it locally).
cases.judgment:
The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) upheld the Controller's
decision to grant India's first-ever Compulsory License to Natco Pharma,
subject to Natco paying a 7% royalty to Bayer.
cases.reasoning:
The IPAB prioritized public health over absolute patent monopolies. The
Board found that Bayer's patient assistance program reached only 2% of
the eligible patient population, proving the public requirement was not
met. Crucially, the IPAB interpreted "reasonably affordable price" from
the perspective of the public, not the patentee's R&D ledger. A price of
₹2.8 lakhs in India was objectively unaffordable. Finally, the Board
established that merely importing a drug does not automatically satisfy
the requirement of "working the patent in India," especially when local
manufacturing could lower costs.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Public Health Exception: The case activated India's compulsory licensing
regime, proving that patent rights are not absolute and must balance with
public health emergencies and affordability.

Affordability Standard: Established that extreme pricing of life-saving
drugs can trigger a compulsory license to generic competitors to ensure
public access.

cases.title: The Chancellor, Masters & Scholars of the University of Oxford v. Rameshwari Photocopy Services
cases.facts:
Major international publishers (Oxford University Press, Cambridge
University Press, etc.) filed a copyright infringement suit against
Rameshwari Photocopy Services, a shop located within the Delhi University
(DU) campus, and DU itself. The shop was compiling course packs-
photocopies of chapters from various copyrighted textbooks-prescribed by
the university syllabus and selling them to students at a nominal cost.
The publishers sought an injunction, arguing this was unauthorized
commercial exploitation of their copyrighted works.
cases.issues:
Does the preparation and sale of course packs comprising photocopied
portions of copyrighted books by a university-sanctioned agent constitute
copyright infringement?

Does this activity fall under the "fair dealing" exception for the
purpose of instruction under Section 52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Publishers)
The publishers argued that the photocopying was not "fair dealing" but a
massive, commercial, institutionalized piracy operation that destroyed
the primary market for their textbooks. They argued that "instruction"
should be limited to a teacher copying a few pages in a classroom, not a
commercial shop printing bound course packs.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Rameshwari Photocopy / Students / DU)
The defendants argued that education in a developing country requires
affordable access to knowledge. They relied on Section 52(1)(i), which
exempts the reproduction of a work "by a teacher or a pupil in the course
of instruction." They argued the photocopy shop was merely acting as an
agent for the students and the university to facilitate this instruction.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Single Judge, later upheld by Division Bench) ruled
in favor of the defendants, dismissing the publishers' suit and
validating the creation of course packs.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment prioritizing educational access.
Justice Endlaw held that copyright is not a divine, natural right, but a
statutory right designed to stimulate creation for the ultimate benefit
of the public. The Court broadly interpreted "in the course of
instruction" under Section 52(1)(i), ruling that it covers the entire
educational process, including preparation for classes. The Court stated
that if a student has the right to photocopy a chapter in the library for
study, the university can employ an agent (the photocopy shop) to do it
efficiently for a whole class. The commercial nature of the shop did not
invalidate the educational purpose of the copying.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Broad Interpretation of Educational Exceptions: India's fair dealing
provisions regarding education are interpreted broadly to encompass
institutional course packs, prioritizing the right to education over
absolute publisher monopolies.

Agency in Fair Dealing: Intermediaries executing the photocopying on
behalf of students/teachers are protected by the same fair dealing
exemptions as the students themselves.

cases.title: Tea Board, India v. ITC Limited
cases.facts:
The Tea Board of India is the registered proprietor of the Geographical
Indication (GI) and the certification trademark for "Darjeeling" tea. ITC
Limited, a major conglomerate, operated a luxury hotel in Kolkata named
"ITC Sonar Bangla," which featured a premium executive lounge named the
"Darjeeling Lounge." The Tea Board sued ITC for infringement of its GI
and certification trademark, arguing that the use of the name
"Darjeeling" for a hotel lounge would confuse consumers and dilute the
distinctiveness of the Darjeeling tea GI.
cases.issues:
Does the protection granted to a Geographical Indication extend to
entirely dissimilar services (like a hotel lounge)?

Can the Tea Board claim trademark dilution or passing off for a
geographical name against a hospitality service?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Tea Board)
The Tea Board argued that "Darjeeling" is a famous mark globally
associated with premium tea. Allowing a luxury hotel to use the name for
its lounge is an attempt to free-ride on the reputation of the GI. They
argued this cross-class use constituted infringement and dilution of the
GI under the Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (ITC Limited)
ITC argued that the GI Act strictly protects goods, not services. A hotel
lounge is a service. Furthermore, there is absolutely no likelihood of
confusion; no consumer would walk into a luxury hotel lounge believing
they are purchasing a packet of raw Darjeeling tea. The name was chosen
to evoke the regional heritage of Bengal, not to sell tea.
cases.judgment:
The Calcutta High Court ruled in favor of ITC Limited, dismissing the Tea
Board's application for an injunction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly construed the limits of Geographical Indication law. A
GI is an indication that identifies goods originating from a specific
territory, where a given quality or reputation is attributable to that
origin. The Court noted that the GI Act does not cover services. Since
ITC was running a hospitality service, there was no infringement under
the GI Act. Furthermore, regarding the trademark dilution claim, the
Court found no cross-class confusion. Darjeeling is a well-known
geographical location in India. The Tea Board does not own a blanket
monopoly over the word "Darjeeling" for all commercial uses, only for
tea.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Statutory Limits of GIs: Geographical Indications in India strictly
protect specific goods, and this protection cannot be stretched to enjoin
the use of geographical names in dissimilar services (like hospitality).

No Absolute Monopoly on Place Names: A certification mark or GI over a
geographic name does not grant the proprietor an absolute monopoly to
prevent all other commercial entities from using that place name in
unrelated contexts.

cases.title: Coca-Cola Company v. Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Bisleri International (formerly Acqua Minerals) created the popular mango
drink "Maaza" and registered the trademark in India. In 1993, Bisleri
sold the "Maaza" trademark, formulation, and intellectual property rights
specifically for the Indian market to the Coca-Cola Company. However,
Bisleri retained the rights to the Maaza mark in foreign countries. Years
later, Coca-Cola discovered that Bisleri had filed for trademark
registration for "Maaza" in Turkey and was exporting Maaza-branded
concentrate from India to be sold abroad. Coca-Cola sued for trademark
infringement and passing off in India, arguing that exporting the goods
from India constituted use of the mark within India.
cases.issues:
Does the manufacture and export of trademarked goods from India
constitute "use" of the trademark within the territory of India, thereby
constituting infringement?

Did Bisleri's actions violate the territorial assignment agreement
transferring the Indian rights to Coca-Cola?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Coca-Cola Company)
Coca-Cola argued that under Section 56 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the
application of a trademark in India on goods intended to be exported from
India constitutes use of the trademark within India. Since Coca-Cola
owned the exclusive rights to the mark in India, Bisleri applying the
mark on export batches inside Indian factories was a direct infringement
of their domestic rights.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Bisleri International)
Bisleri argued that trademark rights are strictly territorial. They had
only assigned the Indian domestic rights to Coca-Cola. Since the actual
sale and commercial exploitation of the exported goods happened in Turkey
(where Bisleri claimed rights), there was no domestic infringement or
passing off within the Indian consumer market.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of the Coca-Cola Company, granting an
interim injunction restraining Bisleri from using the Maaza mark for
exports from India.
cases.reasoning:
The Court relied heavily on the statutory fiction created by Section 56
of the Trade Marks Act. The provision explicitly states that applying a
trademark to goods in India for the purpose of export is deemed to be
"use" of the trademark in India. The Court reasoned that if an entity has
completely assigned its trademark rights within a specific territory
(India), it cannot use that territory as a manufacturing and branding
base, even if the final consumer market is abroad. Bisleri's act of
affixing the "Maaza" label on bottles inside India violated Coca-Cola's
exclusive domestic proprietary rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Export constitutes Domestic Use: Affixing a trademark to goods within
India, even if solely for the purpose of exporting them to a foreign
market, legally constitutes "use" of the trademark within India.

Sanctity of Territorial Assignment: Once a trademark is assigned for a
specific territory, the assignor loses all rights to apply that mark
within that territory, regardless of the goods' final destination.

cases.title: Christian Louboutin Sas v. Pawan Kumar
cases.facts:
Christian Louboutin, a luxury French footwear designer, is globally
famous for incorporating a specific, vibrant "Red Sole" (Pantone 18-1663
TP) on high-heeled women's shoes. Louboutin held a registered trademark
for this red sole in India. The plaintiff discovered that several Indian
footwear merchants (including Pawan Kumar in Delhi) were manufacturing
and selling women's shoes featuring identical red soles. Louboutin sued
for trademark infringement and passing off, claiming the red sole was a
well-known, signature trade dress.
cases.issues:
Can a single color applied to a specific part of a product (a shoe sole)
qualify as a valid, enforceable trademark under the Indian Trade Marks
Act, 1999?

Did the red sole possess sufficient distinctiveness to warrant protection
as a well-known mark?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Christian Louboutin)
The plaintiff argued that the red sole was not functional but purely
decorative and served as a unique source identifier. Over decades of
extensive global marketing and celebrity endorsement, the red sole had
acquired massive secondary meaning. Any consumer seeing a red-soled high
heel immediately associates it with the Louboutin brand.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Pawan Kumar / Merchants)
The defendants argued that color is a basic aesthetic element available
to all designers. Granting a monopoly over the color red on a shoe sole
stifles competition in the fashion industry. They argued that under the
Trade Marks Act, a single color cannot be monopolized unless it is a
combination of colors.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Christian Louboutin, granting a
permanent injunction against the defendants and recognizing the red sole
as a well-known trademark.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Mukta Gupta delivered a progressive ruling on non-traditional
trademarks. The Court noted that the definition of a trademark under
Section 2(m) of the Act includes "combination of colours," but
jurisprudence has evolved to recognize single colors if they have
acquired immense distinctiveness. The Court found that Louboutin's red
sole had become iconic. The extensive evidence of sales, advertising, and
pop-culture references proved that the specific red color on the outsole
had acquired a "secondary meaning" in the minds of consumers. It
functioned exclusively as a badge of origin. Therefore, copying it was a
deliberate attempt to pass off ordinary shoes as luxury goods.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Protection of Single Color Marks: Indian trademark law can protect a
single color applied to a specific position on a product, provided the
plaintiff can prove overwhelming acquired distinctiveness and secondary
meaning (non-traditional trademarks).

Trade Dress in Fashion: Establishes strong protection for iconic, non-
functional design elements in the fashion and luxury goods sectors
against counterfeiters.

cases.title: Bharat Glass Tube Limited v. Gopal Glass Works Limited
cases.facts:
Gopal Glass Works had registered a specific design (a diamond-shaped
pattern with specific optical properties) for figured glass sheets in
India. They discovered that Bharat Glass Tube was manufacturing and
marketing glass sheets with an identical design. Gopal Glass sued for
design infringement. Bharat Glass counter-sued, seeking the cancellation
of Gopal Glass's registration. Bharat Glass argued that the design lacked
novelty because the exact design had been previously published in a
German catalogue by a company named M/s. Walther Glas, and had been used
in the UK before it was registered in India.
cases.issues:
What constitutes "prior publication" to defeat the novelty of a
registered design under the Designs Act, 2000?

Does the mere existence of a design in a foreign catalogue accessible in
India destroy novelty?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Bharat Glass Tube)
Bharat Glass argued that novelty is an absolute global requirement. Since
the design was printed in a German catalogue (which was deposited in the
UK Patent Office and accessible to the public), the design was already in
the public domain. Therefore, Gopal Glass's registration was invalid for
lacking originality and novelty.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Gopal Glass Works)
Gopal Glass argued that they were the original creators of this specific
application of the design onto glass sheets in India. They argued that
the German catalogue was highly obscure, and there was no evidence that
it had actually been circulated or viewed by anyone in the relevant trade
in India prior to their registration.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Gopal Glass Works, upholding
the validity of their design registration and confirming the infringement
by Bharat Glass.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court clarified the strict standard required to prove "prior
publication." The Court held that for a document or catalogue to destroy
novelty, it is not enough that the document simply exists somewhere in
the world. The publication must be of such a nature that the design is
disclosed to the public in a tangible way. The party claiming prior
publication must prove that the specific design had been published and
was accessible to the public or the relevant trade in India. Because
Bharat Glass could only prove that an obscure German catalogue existed in
a UK library, but failed to prove that it had been imported, circulated,
or read by anyone in India's glass industry before Gopal Glass filed
their registration, the defense of prior publication failed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Standard for Prior Publication: To defeat a design's novelty based on a
prior document, there must be clear evidence that the document was
actually accessible to the public or the relevant trade within the
jurisdiction; obscure foreign existence is insufficient.

Application of Design to Article: Novelty requires looking at the design
as applied to the specific article (glass sheets), not just as an
abstract pattern on paper.

cases.title: Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Sundial Communications Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Sundial Communications, a television production house, developed a highly
original concept, character sketch, and detailed script for a television
show titled Krish Kanhaiya. They pitched this concept to Zee Telefilms
under conditions of strict confidentiality, sharing detailed notes and
character profiles. Zee initially expressed interest but later rejected
the proposal. Shortly after, Zee launched its own television show titled
Kanhaiya, which heavily borrowed the core concept, character traits, and
specific narrative arcs pitched by Sundial. Sundial sued Zee for
copyright infringement and breach of confidentiality.
cases.issues:
Can there be copyright in an unproduced idea, concept, or television
format?

What are the legal elements required to establish a breach of confidence
in the entertainment industry regarding pitched ideas?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Sundial Communications)
Sundial acknowledged the basic rule that there is no copyright in a mere
idea. However, they argued that their pitch was not a vague idea, but a
fully developed "format" and script. Furthermore, they argued that Zee
received this information in a commercial context implying strict
confidentiality, and using it without permission was a breach of
equitable trust.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Zee Telefilms)
Zee argued the classic defense: ideas cannot be copyrighted. They claimed
the concept of a modern-day Lord Krishna helping a protagonist is a
common mythological trope in India and belongs in the public domain. They
argued that any similarities were coincidental based on common themes
(Scènes à faire).
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court ruled in favor of Sundial Communications, granting
an injunction against Zee Telefilms from broadcasting the infringing
show.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a crucial judgment protecting original concepts in
the media industry. While reiterating that copyright protects the
expression of an idea, not the idea itself, the Court held that if an
idea is developed into a detailed format, treatment, or character sketch,
it crosses the threshold into protectable expression. More importantly,
the Court ruled on the Law of Confidence. Even if the copyright claim was
weak, equity protects confidential information. The Court established a
three-prong test for breach of confidence: (1) the information must have
the necessary quality of confidence (it was original and not public
knowledge); (2) it must have been imparted in circumstances importing an
obligation of confidence (a commercial pitch); and (3) there must be an
unauthorized use of that information to the detriment of the party
communicating it. Zee failed this test spectacularly.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Breach of Confidentiality (Trade Secrets): Equitable protection exists
for business concepts and TV formats pitched in confidence, independent
of formal copyright law.

Idea vs. Expression: While generic ideas are unprotectable, a fully
fleshed-out, detailed structural format of a show enjoys legal protection
against misappropriation.

cases.title: PepsiCo India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Kavitha Kuruganti
cases.facts:
PepsiCo India holds a registered certificate under the Protection of
Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 (PPV&FR Act) for a specific
variety of potato (FL-2027, known as FC5). This variety has low moisture
content, making it ideal for Lay's potato chips. PepsiCo operates a
contract-farming model, supplying seeds to licensed farmers who sell the
crop back. In 2019, PepsiCo discovered that several unlicensed
smallholder farmers in Gujarat were growing and selling the FC5 variety.
PepsiCo sued the farmers for intellectual property infringement. Public
outrage ensued, and Kavitha Kuruganti, an activist, filed an application
before the PPV&FR Authority to revoke PepsiCo's registration, arguing
that suing small farmers violated the statutory rights granted to them
under the Act.
cases.issues:
Do the rights of a plant breeder (PepsiCo) override the traditional
rights of farmers to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, or sell farm
produce under the PPV&FR Act?

Were the grounds for revocation of PepsiCo's plant variety certificate
satisfied?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Kuruganti / Farmers' Rights Advocates)
The activists argued that Section 39(1)(iv) of the PPV&FR Act grants
overriding protection to farmers. The section explicitly states that a
farmer is entitled to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, or sell his
farm produce including seed of a variety protected under this Act,
provided they do not sell branded seed. They argued PepsiCo's lawsuits
were a harassment tactic violating public interest, which is a statutory
ground for revoking a certificate.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (PepsiCo India)
PepsiCo argued that they had invested heavily in developing the FC5
variety. While acknowledging farmers' rights, they argued that commercial
cultivation of their protected variety by unlicensed farmers for
supplying to rival chip manufacturers destroyed their commercial monopoly
and undermined the breeder's rights the Act was designed to protect.
cases.judgment:
The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Authority ruled in
favor of the farmers/activists, revoking PepsiCo's registration for the
FL-2027 potato variety. (This was later upheld by the Delhi High Court).
cases.reasoning:
The Authority and the Court rigorously enforced the unique, pro-farmer
architecture of India's intellectual property regime regarding
agriculture. Unlike western IP regimes, the Indian PPV&FR Act uniquely
balances breeder rights with farmers' rights. The Authority found that
PepsiCo had filed lawsuits against small farmers to intimidate them,
which was contrary to the public interest. The judgment solidified that
Section 39 creates an absolute right for farmers to grow and sell any
protected variety of crop, so long as they are not selling it as "branded
seed" in a packaged form. Because the farmers were selling the potatoes
as raw produce, not branded seeds, PepsiCo's aggressive infringement
suits violated the spirit of the legislation, warranting revocation of
their IP right.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Supremacy of Farmers' Rights: In Indian IP law, the right of a farmer to
save, sow, and sell the produce of a protected plant variety (unbranded)
overrides the commercial monopoly of the corporate plant breeder.

Public Interest Revocation: Using intellectual property litigation to
harass smallholder farmers constitutes acting against the "public
interest," serving as valid grounds to revoke a plant variety
registration.

cases.title: R.G. Anand v. Delux Films
cases.facts:
R.G. Anand, a playwright, wrote a stage play titled Hum Hindustani, which
dealt with the evils of provincialism and the need for national
integration. The play was a major success. Anand subsequently met with
the defendants (Delux Films) to discuss adapting the play into a motion
picture, providing them with the script. While no agreement was reached,
Delux Films later released a movie titled New Delhi, which also revolved
around the theme of provincialism and featured a romance between a North
Indian and a South Indian. Anand sued for copyright infringement,
claiming the movie was a direct adaptation of his play.
cases.issues:
Does copyright law protect the underlying idea, theme, or plot of a
literary work?

What is the legal standard for determining if a subsequent work
constitutes a "colorable imitation" or substantial infringement of the
original work?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (R.G. Anand)
Anand argued that the defendants had direct access to his manuscript. He
listed numerous similarities in the character arcs, the central conflict
(provincial prejudice in marriage), and the ultimate resolution, arguing
that the movie was a blatant, unauthorized cinematographic adaptation of
his original literary work.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Delux Films)
The defendants argued that the theme of provincialism and cross-cultural
marriage in India is a common socio-political reality, not an original
concept belonging to the plaintiff. They contended that while the broad
theme was identical, the treatment, screenplay, dialogue, and climax of
the movie were entirely distinct and original.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Delux Films, dismissing the
copyright infringement suit.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court delivered the most authoritative Indian ruling on the
Idea-Expression Dichotomy. The Court held that there can be no copyright
in an idea, subject matter, theme, or historical fact; copyright only
extends to the unique form, manner, and arrangement of the expression of
that idea. To determine infringement, the Court laid down the "Lay
Observer Test": if an ordinary, reasonable person, after reading the play
and watching the movie, gets the unmistakable impression that the movie
is a copy of the play, infringement exists. The Court found that while
both works shared the same broad idea, the movie's treatment, sub-plots,
and execution were materially different.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Idea-Expression Dichotomy: Solidified the universal principle that ideas
are free for all to use; only the original expression of an idea is
protected by copyright.

Lay Observer Test: Established the objective standard for determining
substantial similarity and copyright infringement in Indian courts.

cases.title: Yahoo! Inc. v. Akash Arora & Anr.
cases.facts:
Yahoo! Inc., the global internet giant, owned the widely recognized
trademark and domain name "Yahoo.com". The defendants, Akash Arora and
his company, launched a localized internet portal providing similar
services (web directory, search) under the domain name "Yahooindia.com".
Yahoo! Inc. filed a suit for passing off in the Delhi High Court, seeking
an injunction to stop the defendants from using the phonetically and
visually identical domain name.
cases.issues:
Can a domain name be legally protected as a trademark under the action of
passing off?

Does adding a geographical suffix (like "india") to a well-known global
mark sufficiently distinguish the subsequent mark to avoid consumer
confusion?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Yahoo! Inc.)
Yahoo argued that their mark was globally renowned and possessed massive
trans-border reputation extending into India. They contended that domain
names are not merely addresses but function as vital corporate
identifiers (trademarks). Using "Yahooindia.com" was a deliberate attempt
to hijack their brand equity and confuse internet users into believing
the site was an official Indian branch of Yahoo.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Akash Arora)
The defendants argued that "Yahoo" is a general dictionary word, and
trademark laws applicable to physical goods cannot be directly
transplanted to the internet. They also argued that internet users are
highly sophisticated and would not confuse "Yahooindia.com" with the
global "Yahoo.com".
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Yahoo! Inc., granting an interim
injunction against the defendants and recognizing domain names as
protectable trademarks.
cases.reasoning:
The Court was one of the first in India to deal with cybersquatting and
domain name disputes. The Court flatly rejected the argument that
internet users are too sophisticated to be confused. In the digital
realm, domain names serve the exact same function as a physical
trademark-they identify the source of the service. Because "Yahoo" had
acquired immense distinctiveness, the addition of the word "india" did
not cure the infringement; rather, it actively increased the likelihood
of confusion by making users think it was a regional subsidiary. The
Court applied the traditional principles of passing off to the cyberspace
environment.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Domain Names as Trademarks: Established that internet domain names are
entitled to the exact same legal protection against passing off as
physical trademarks.

Cybersquatting Protection: Paved the way for robust protection of
international brands against localized domain name hijackers in India.

cases.title: N.R. Dongre v. Whirlpool Corporation
cases.facts:
Whirlpool Corporation, a US-based multinational, had registered the
trademark "WHIRLPOOL" in India in 1956 but allowed the registration to
lapse in 1977 due to non-renewal. Despite the lapse, Whirlpool continued
to advertise globally (including in magazines circulating in India) and
sold machines to US embassies in India. In 1986, an Indian trust
(represented by N.R. Dongre) registered the mark "WHIRLPOOL" for washing
machines and began manufacturing them. Whirlpool Corp. sued the Indian
entity for passing off, despite not having a valid Indian registration at
the time.
cases.issues:
Can a foreign entity maintain an action for passing off in India even if
it does not have a registered trademark or actual physical sales within
the Indian territory?

Does global advertising constitute sufficient "use" to establish a
reputation within a specific national jurisdiction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Respondent (Whirlpool Corp.)
Whirlpool argued that trademark rights are not strictly limited to
physical borders. Through extensive global marketing, circulation of
foreign magazines in India, and word-of-mouth, the WHIRLPOOL mark had
acquired a massive "trans-border reputation" in India. The Indian
entity's adoption of the exact mark was a bad-faith attempt to trade on
Whirlpool's global goodwill.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Appellant (N.R. Dongre)
Dongre argued the strict territoriality principle: a trademark only
exists where it is registered and physically used. Since Whirlpool
abandoned its Indian registration and had no commercial sales to Indian
consumers, they had zero goodwill in India. As the registered owners of
the mark in India, Dongre claimed the absolute right to use it.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Whirlpool Corporation,
granting an injunction against the Indian registered trademark holder
based on the tort of passing off.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court decisively adopted the doctrine of Trans-Border
Reputation. The Court held that physical presence or local manufacturing
is not a mandatory prerequisite to establish goodwill. In an era of
global communication, international travel, and cross-border media, a
brand's reputation travels faster than its goods. Because Whirlpool's
advertisements reached Indian shores, the brand had established a
protectable reputation among Indian consumers. An action for passing off
is based on common law equity to prevent fraud and consumer confusion;
therefore, it can override a local statutory trademark registration if
that local registration was acquired in bad faith to exploit an
internationally famous mark.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Trans-Border Reputation Doctrine: A foreign trademark owner can enforce
their rights in India through a passing-off action even without formal
registration or physical commercial presence, provided the mark's global
reputation has spilled over into the Indian market.

cases.title: F. Hoffmann-La Roche Ltd. v. Cipla Ltd.
cases.facts:
Hoffmann-La Roche, a Swiss pharmaceutical company, held a valid Indian
patent for the cancer drug Erlotinib (marketed as Tarceva), which cost
approximately ₹1.4 lakhs per month. Cipla, an Indian generic
manufacturer, launched a generic version of Erlotinib (marketed as
Erlocip) at a fraction of the cost (₹4,600 per month). Roche filed a suit
for patent infringement in the Delhi High Court and sought a temporary
injunction to immediately halt Cipla from manufacturing and selling the
generic drug pending the final trial.
cases.issues:
In pharmaceutical patent infringement cases, should courts grant interim
injunctions purely based on the existence of a valid patent?

What role does "public interest" (specifically the pricing and
availability of life-saving drugs) play in the equitable relief of
granting an injunction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Hoffmann-La Roche)
Roche argued the traditional patent position: a patent grants an absolute
statutory monopoly. Cipla was blatantly infringing on their valid patent.
Failing to grant an interim injunction would destroy Roche's market
exclusivity and set a dangerous precedent, discouraging future R&D
investments in life-saving drugs.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Cipla Ltd.)
Cipla challenged the validity of the patent (a standard defense). More
importantly, they relied on the "balance of convenience" and "irreparable
injury" tests for injunctions. They argued that stopping the generic drug
would deprive thousands of cancer patients of an affordable, life-saving
treatment, causing irreparable harm to the public.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled in favor of Cipla, denying
Roche's request for an interim injunction, allowing Cipla to continue
selling the generic drug during the trial. (Note: Roche eventually won
the final trial years later, but the interim denial was historic).
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a groundbreaking ruling that fundamentally altered
the landscape of pharmaceutical patent litigation in India. The Court
held that an interim injunction is an equitable remedy, not an automatic
statutory right. The courts must weigh the "balance of convenience." In
cases involving life-saving medical therapies, the Court ruled that the
"public interest" is a mandatory factor. The massive price disparity
(₹1.4 lakhs vs. ₹4,600) meant that granting the injunction would result
in the deaths of patients who could not afford Roche's drug. The
irreparable harm to the public far outweighed the purely financial harm
to Roche (which could be compensated by damages if Roche won the final
trial).
cases.legalPrinciples:
Public Interest in Injunctions: Established that in India, the
enforcement of pharmaceutical patents via interim injunctions is
subordinate to the right to life and public health; extreme price
disparities justify denying preliminary injunctions to patentees.

cases.title: Dimminaco A.G. v. Controller of Patents and Designs
cases.facts:
Dimminaco A.G., a Swiss company, developed a process for preparing a live
vaccine for Bursitis (a poultry disease). The end product of this
specific process contained a living organism (a live virus). The Indian
Patent Office rejected the patent application. The Examiner argued that
because the end product contained a "living organism," it was not a non-
living tangible substance, and therefore the process did not result in an
"article" or "substance" qualifying as an "invention" or "manner of
manufacture" under Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act, 1970.
cases.issues:
Can a manufacturing process be denied a patent solely because the final
end-product contains a living organism?

Does a process that utilizes living entities fall within the legal
definition of a "manner of manufacture"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Dimminaco A.G.)
Dimminaco argued that the Patents Act did not explicitly bar the
patentability of processes merely because the end product was a living
virus. They argued the process itself was novel, involved an inventive
step (it required specific, controlled conditions), and had immense
industrial application (veterinary medicine), fulfilling all statutory
criteria for a process patent.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Controller of Patents)
The Controller relied on traditional, conservative patent doctrines,
arguing that "manufacture" historically implies transforming inanimate
matter into a new inanimate article. Because a live virus occurs in
nature and is a living entity, the process of isolating or preparing it
does not equate to "manufacturing" a new substance.
cases.judgment:
The Calcutta High Court ruled in favor of Dimminaco A.G., overturning the
Patent Office's rejection and directing them to reconsider the
application.
cases.reasoning:
The High Court modernized Indian patent law to accommodate biotechnology.
The Court noted that the term "manufacture" was not rigidly defined in
the Act. Since the statute did not expressly exclude processes producing
living organisms, the Patent Office was wrong to read such an exclusion
into the law. The Court applied the "Vendibility Test": if the process
results in a new and useful product that is commercially viable and can
be sold (vendible), it qualifies as a manner of manufacture. The vaccine
was highly useful and commercially successful; the fact that it achieved
its utility via a live virus was irrelevant to the patentability of the
process that created it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Biotech Patentability: Marked the genesis of biotechnology patenting in
India, establishing that a process is not disqualified from patent
protection merely because it involves or produces living organisms,
provided it meets the standard tests of novelty, utility, and non-
obviousness.

cases.title: Super Cassettes Industries Ltd. v. MySpace Inc.
cases.facts:
Super Cassettes Industries (T-Series), India's largest music label, sued
MySpace, a major social networking and user-generated content platform.
T-Series claimed that MySpace users were illegally uploading thousands of
T-Series' copyrighted songs and music videos. T-Series argued that by
providing a platform, adding advertisements, and formatting the uploaded
videos, MySpace was actively participating in and monetizing copyright
infringement. MySpace claimed immunity as a mere "intermediary" under the
Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
cases.issues:
Does the safe harbor protection for intermediaries under Section 79 of
the IT Act override the strict liability for infringement under Section
51 of the Copyright Act?

What level of "knowledge" is required to hold an online intermediary
liable for user-generated copyright infringement?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Super Cassettes / T-Series)
T-Series argued that the Copyright Act is a special statute that takes
precedence. Under copyright law, authorizing infringement is illegal. By
giving users the tools to upload and share music, MySpace was authorizing
piracy. They argued MySpace should be forced to pre-screen all uploads to
prevent infringement before it happens.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (MySpace Inc.)
MySpace argued that as an intermediary handling massive volumes of data,
pre-screening was technologically impossible and would destroy the
internet. They relied on Section 79 of the IT Act, which grants immunity
to platforms if they observe due diligence and take down infringing
content after receiving actual knowledge (a takedown notice).
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled in favor of MySpace,
harmonizing the IT Act and the Copyright Act, and establishing a "notice
and takedown" regime.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a vital balance between protecting IP and protecting
internet intermediaries. The Court held that Section 79 of the IT Act
does apply to copyright infringement. It provides a safe harbor, meaning
intermediaries are not strictly liable for user content. Crucially, the
Court defined "actual knowledge." An intermediary does not have "actual
knowledge" of infringement just because it knows piracy generally happens
on its site. Actual knowledge only arises when the copyright owner
provides a specific, precise URL/link to the infringing content (a
takedown notice). Once the specific notice is received, the platform must
remove it within 36 hours. The Court ruled that forcing platforms to pre-
screen content would lead to private censorship and choke free speech.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Intermediary Safe Harbor: Online platforms (ISPs, social media) are
shielded from secondary copyright infringement liabilities provided they
act expeditiously to remove content upon receiving specific, targeted
takedown notices from rights holders.

Actual Knowledge Standard: General awareness of piracy is insufficient to
trigger liability; copyright owners bear the burden of identifying
specific infringing URLs.

cases.title: Milmet Oftho Industries v. Allergan Inc.
cases.facts:
Allergan Inc., an international pharmaceutical company, coined the
trademark "OCUFLOX" for an eye-care drug and sold it in numerous
countries globally, though it had not launched the drug or registered the
mark in India. Milmet Oftho, an Indian pharmaceutical company,
subsequently adopted the identical trademark "OCUFLOX" for an identical
eye-care drug and registered it in India. Allergan sued Milmet for
passing off, claiming prior global use. Milmet argued they were the
honest, prior users within the territory of India.
cases.issues:
In the context of pharmaceutical products, who prevails in a trademark
dispute: the first entity to use the mark globally, or the first entity
to use the mark locally in India?

Do medicinal products require a stricter standard of trademark protection
to prevent consumer confusion?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Milmet Oftho Industries)
Milmet argued the standard territoriality principle. Since Allergan did
not sell OCUFLOX in India and had no Indian registration, Milmet was the
first true user in the Indian market. They argued they coined the term
independently and should not be punished for Allergan's failure to enter
the Indian market sooner.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Allergan Inc.)
Allergan argued trans-border reputation. Medical professionals read
international journals and attend global conferences. Therefore, doctors
in India were highly aware of the global OCUFLOX brand. Allowing an
Indian company to use the identical mark for an identical drug would lead
to disastrous medical confusion.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Allergan Inc., granting an
injunction against the Indian company.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court established a highly protective standard specifically
tailored for pharmaceutical trademarks. The Court held that when dealing
with medicines, the standard for confusion is not the ordinary consumer,
but the potential for disastrous health consequences. The Court
established the "First in the World Market" rule for pharmaceuticals. If
a multinational company is the first to introduce a drug globally under a
specific mark, an Indian company cannot later adopt the exact same mark
for the same drug, even if the Indian company is the first to launch
locally. The global nature of medical knowledge means trans-border
reputation is easily established, and preventing any chance of dispensing
the wrong medicine to a patient is paramount.
cases.legalPrinciples:
First in the World Market Rule: In pharmaceutical trademark disputes,
global prior use heavily outweighs local territorial prior use,
effectively expanding the trans-border reputation doctrine to protect
global drug brands from local appropriation.

Stricter Scrutiny for Medicines: Courts will apply a much lower threshold
for likelihood of confusion in trademark cases involving medicinal
products to protect public health.

cases.title: Gramophone Co. of India Ltd. v. Birendra Bahadur Pandey
cases.facts:
The Gramophone Company of India (HMV) held the copyright for numerous
audio recordings. An unauthorized consignment of pirated audio cassettes
containing HMV's copyrighted music arrived at the Calcutta Port. The
consignment originated from Singapore and was destined for Kathmandu,
Nepal. The goods were merely in transit through Indian territory and were
not meant for the Indian commercial market. HMV approached the Registrar
of Copyrights and the Customs authorities to seize the goods, arguing
that bringing the pirated cassettes into India constituted "importation"
and therefore copyright infringement. The consignee argued that goods in
transit are not "imported."
cases.issues:
Does the word "import" in the Copyright Act, 1957, include goods that are
merely passing through Indian territory (in transit) to a foreign
destination?

Can Indian customs authorities seize pirated goods that are not intended
for commerce within India?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Gramophone Co. of India)
HMV argued for a literal interpretation of the word "import"-meaning to
bring into the country from outside. The moment the pirated cassettes
crossed the territorial waters and landed at the Calcutta Port, they were
imported. Allowing India to be used as a safe transit route for
international piracy violates India's obligations under international
copyright treaties.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Birendra Bahadur Pandey / Consignee)
The respondents relied on customs jurisprudence, arguing that "import"
means bringing goods into a country for the purpose of mixing them into
the mass of property in that country (i.e., for local consumption). Since
the goods were destined for Nepal under a treaty of transit, they were
legally never "imported" into India's commercial stream.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the Gramophone Company,
holding that transit goods are subject to Indian copyright law.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court provided a purposive interpretation of the Copyright
Act. The Court held that the word "import" is not restricted to bringing
goods in for local commerce. In the context of copyright infringement,
"import" simply means bringing a work into India from outside India,
regardless of the ultimate destination. The primary purpose of the
Copyright Act is to prevent the proliferation of pirated goods. To adopt
the narrow customs definition of "import" would essentially force India
to facilitate international piracy, violating international conventions.
Therefore, even pirated goods merely in transit through Indian ports can
be seized by the authorities.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Broad Definition of Importation: In Indian IP law, the physical entry of
infringing goods into Indian territorial limits constitutes
"importation," regardless of whether the goods are meant for local sale
or are in transit to another sovereign nation.

Border Enforcement against Piracy: Empowers rights holders to use Indian
customs mechanisms to choke international piracy supply chains that pass
through India.

cases.title: Star India Pvt. Ltd. v. Leo Burnett (India) Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Star India broadcasted an immensely popular television soap opera titled
Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi. The main characters, "Tulsi" and
"Savita," became household names across India. Leo Burnett, an
advertising agency representing Procter & Gamble, created a television
commercial for "Tide" detergent. The commercial featured lookalike actors
mimicking the distinct mannerisms, traditional attire, and character
dynamics of Tulsi and Savita. Star India sued for copyright infringement
and passing off, claiming the ad agency had stolen the intellectual
property associated with their fictional characters.
cases.issues:
Does Indian copyright law recognize and protect the standalone
"merchandising rights" or copyright in fictional characters independent
of the script/video?

Did the advertisement constitute passing off by creating a false
association with the TV show?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Star India)
Star India argued that the characters Tulsi and Savita had transcended
the show and acquired independent, massive commercial value. They claimed
the creators of the show owned the exclusive "character merchandising
rights." The Tide commercial exploited this specific character equity
without authorization, confusing the public into believing Star India had
endorsed the detergent.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Leo Burnett)
The ad agency argued that there is no independent copyright in generic
character tropes (the traditional Indian mother-in-law and daughter-in-
law). They argued the commercial was a legal parody/satire. Furthermore,
they did not use the actual names of the characters, so there was no
direct copyright infringement of the scripts, only a comedic homage.
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court denied the interim injunction, ruling that while
character merchandising rights exist, they were not definitively
infringed in this specific instance.
cases.reasoning:
This case officially recognized Character Merchandising in Indian
jurisprudence. The Court acknowledged that fictional characters can
indeed acquire an independent life and commercial value protectable under
copyright and passing off. However, the Court applied a strict standard:
for a character to be copyrightable independently, it must be uniquely
distinct and specifically identifiable (like Mickey Mouse or James Bond).
The Court found that "Tulsi" and "Savita," while popular, were
essentially generic portrayals of traditional Indian women. Because the
ad used lookalikes in a parody setting and didn't directly steal
dialogue, the threshold for copyright infringement wasn't met. However,
the Court firmly laid down that unauthorized commercial exploitation of
truly unique characters constitutes a violation of character
merchandising rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Recognition of Character Merchandising: Established that the creators of
distinct, well-defined fictional characters hold exclusive commercial
rights to exploit those characters, preventing unauthorized brand
endorsements.

Threshold of Distinctiveness: Fictional characters based on generic
cultural tropes face a high burden of proof to claim independent
copyright protection outside of their specific storylines.

cases.title: Amarnath Sehgal v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Amarnath Sehgal, a world-renowned sculptor, was commissioned by the
Government of India in the 1950s to create a massive bronze mural for the
lobby of Vigyan Bhavan, a premier international convention center in New
Delhi. The mural was a masterpiece and a national landmark. Decades
later, during renovations, government officials unceremoniously ripped
the mural off the wall, dismantled it, and dumped the pieces into a
storeroom, causing severe damage to the artwork. Sehgal, deeply aggrieved
by the destruction of his life's work, sued the Government under Section
57 of the Copyright Act, claiming a violation of his "Moral Rights."
cases.issues:
Do the "Moral Rights" (paternity and integrity) of an author survive even
after the economic rights (copyright) and the physical ownership of the
artwork have been transferred to the buyer (the Government)?

Can an author demand damages and the return of a damaged artwork from its
legal owner based on the violation of the right of integrity?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Amarnath Sehgal)
Sehgal argued that Section 57 of the Copyright Act grants authors
special, inalienable moral rights independent of economic copyright. The
right to "integrity" allows an author to restrain any distortion,
mutilation, or modification of their work that would prejudice their
honor or reputation. Tearing down and dumping the mural was the ultimate
mutilation, deeply harming his artistic legacy.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Union of India)
The Government argued property law. They had commissioned the work and
paid for it. They were the absolute legal owners of the physical bronze
mural. As owners, they had the right to display it, store it, or even
destroy it. They argued that Section 57 prevents modification, but
complete removal and storage do not constitute modification.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled emphatically in favor of Amarnath Sehgal,
upholding his moral rights, awarding him damages, and ordering the
Government to return the remains of the mural to him.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Pradeep Nandrajog delivered a poetic and landmark judgment on the
soul of copyright law. The Court held that an artist's creation is an
extension of their personality. Therefore, Moral Rights (Droit Moral) are
absolute, perpetual, and cannot be bought or extinguished by transferring
physical ownership or economic copyright. The Court ruled that
"mutilation" under Section 57 is not just physical alteration; pulling
down a site-specific mural and reducing it to scrap inherently destroys
the artistic integrity of the work and slaughters the artist's
reputation. The Government's ownership of the bronze metal did not give
them the right to destroy the intangible soul of the artwork.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Supremacy of Moral Rights: Established that an author's right to
paternity and integrity (Section 57) exists independently of economic
copyright and binds the legal owner of the physical work.

Protection Against Destruction: Interpreted the right of integrity to
mean that the destruction, improper removal, or severe mutilation of an
artwork constitutes a legal injury to the artist's honor, actionable for
damages and restitution.

cases.title: Bajaj Auto Ltd. v. TVS Motor Company Ltd.
cases.facts:
Bajaj Auto held a patent for "DTS-i" (Digital Twin Spark Ignition)
technology, which improved fuel efficiency in small internal combustion
engines by using two spark plugs. TVS Motor Company launched a motorcycle
named "Flame," which featured a "CC-VTI" engine utilizing a twin-spark
plug configuration. Bajaj sued TVS for patent infringement and sought an
interim injunction. The litigation resulted in a prolonged battle of
injunctions and counter-injunctions spanning multiple courts, stalling
the launch of the product for years without reaching a final trial.
cases.issues:
Does the use of two spark plugs in a different configuration by TVS
infringe upon Bajaj's DTS-i patent?

How should courts handle interim injunctions in complex intellectual
property disputes to prevent the indefinite stalling of commercial
products?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Bajaj Auto Ltd.)
Bajaj argued that their patent covered the fundamental concept and
specific implementation of using two spark plugs in an internal
combustion engine of a specific size to achieve leaner fuel burns. They
argued TVS's CC-VTI technology was a direct, mechanical equivalent
(colorable imitation) of their patented DTS-i technology, infringing on
their statutory monopoly.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (TVS Motor Company)
TVS argued that the concept of twin spark plugs was old and known in the
prior art (e.g., Honda had used it previously). They argued their CC-VTI
technology had a distinct configuration featuring three valves, which was
materially different from Bajaj's two-valve DTS-i system, meaning there
was no infringement.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India directed the lower courts to expedite the
trial and heavily criticized the practice of deciding IP matters solely
at the interim injunction stage. (The parties eventually settled out of
court).
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court used this case to lay down sweeping procedural reforms
for Indian IP litigation. The Court observed that intellectual property
disputes, particularly patents and trademarks, were being fought almost
entirely at the temporary injunction stage. These injunctions would drag
on for years, effectively destroying the commercial lifecycle of a
product before the actual evidence was even examined in a full trial. The
Court mandated that in matters relating to trademarks, copyright, and
patents, courts must conduct the final trial on a day-to-day basis and
conclude it within four months of filing, rather than granting indefinite
interim injunctions based on prima facie assumptions.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Expedited IP Trials: Established a mandatory judicial directive
prioritizing rapid, day-to-day final trials for intellectual property
disputes over the granting of prolonged interim injunctions.

Commercial Lifecycles: Recognized that in technology and IP, a delayed
trial equates to denied justice due to the rapid obsolescence of
commercial products.

cases.title: Monsanto Technology LLC v. Nuziveedu Seeds Ltd.
cases.facts:
Monsanto developed and patented a biotechnological invention: the Cry2Ab
DNA construct (derived from Bacillus thuringiensis). When inserted into
plant cells, this genetic construct made cotton plants resistant to
bollworm. Monsanto licensed this technology to Indian seed companies
(including Nuziveedu). Following a royalty dispute, Nuziveedu terminated
the agreement but continued using the technology. Monsanto sued for
patent infringement. Nuziveedu counter-sued, arguing that Monsanto's
patent was invalid under Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, which prohibits
the patenting of "plants and animals in whole or any part thereof
including seeds."
cases.issues:
Does a genetically modified DNA construct (a nucleic acid sequence) fall
under the exclusion of "plants, seeds, or parts thereof" under Section
3(j) of the Patents Act?

Can a patent be granted for a biotechnology process that is eventually
integrated into a plant variety?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Monsanto Technology LLC)
Monsanto argued that they were not patenting a plant or a seed. They
patented an isolated, synthesized DNA construct created in a laboratory.
This DNA sequence is a man-made chemical compound. The fact that it is
later inserted into a plant cell by seed companies does not retroactively
transform the laboratory invention into a "plant part" disqualified under
Section 3(j).

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Nuziveedu Seeds Ltd.)
Nuziveedu argued that the DNA sequence has no standalone industrial
application; it only works when integrated into a cotton seed. Once
inserted, it becomes an inseparable, biological part of the plant trait.
Therefore, it is a "part of a plant" and inherently unpatentable under
Section 3(j). They argued Monsanto should seek protection under the Plant
Varieties Act, not patent law.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India restored Monsanto's patent (overturning the
Division Bench of the High Court) and remanded the matter back to the
trial court for a full technical trial.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court held that the Division Bench of the High Court erred by
invalidating a highly complex biotechnology patent at the summary/interim
stage without expert evidence. The Court ruled that the question of
whether an isolated DNA construct acts as a chemical compound or
biologically fuses to become an unpatentable "part of a plant" is a
profound scientific inquiry. It cannot be decided based purely on legal
semantics during injunction hearings. By restoring the patent pending a
full trial, the Supreme Court implicitly signaled that isolated genetic
sequences developed in a lab do not automatically fall under the Section
3(j) exclusion just because they are eventually used in agriculture.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Biotech Patents & Agriculture: Reaffirmed that isolated genetic sequences
(DNA constructs) maintain their status as patentable inventions distinct
from the biological plants they are inserted into, protecting biotech R&D
in the agricultural sector.

Evidentiary Threshold for Invalidation: Complex scientific patents cannot
be revoked summarily; invalidation under Section 3(j) requires rigorous
expert testimony during a full trial.

cases.title: Indian Performing Right Society Ltd. (IPRS) v. Eastern India Motion Picture Association (EIMPA)
cases.facts:
The IPRS, a copyright society representing music composers and lyricists,
demanded royalties from cinema hall owners whenever films containing
their members' songs were exhibited publicly. The Eastern India Motion
Picture Association (representing film producers) objected. The producers
argued that when a composer writes a song specifically to be incorporated
into a cinematograph film, the film producer becomes the first owner of
the copyright for the entire film, which includes the music. Therefore,
composers lose the right to demand separate public performance royalties
when the film is screened.
cases.issues:
Does the composer of a musical work retain independent copyright in the
music once it is incorporated into a cinematograph film?

Who is the first owner of copyright when a musical work is commissioned
specifically for a movie?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (IPRS / Composers)
IPRS argued that a song comprises distinct copyrights: the literary work
(lyrics) and the musical work (melody). While the producer owns the
copyright to the cinematograph film (the visual recording), the composers
retain their underlying rights. Therefore, broadcasting the music
requires a separate license from the composers.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (EIMPA / Producers)
The producers relied on Section 17(b) & (c) of the Copyright Act. They
argued that when an author is commissioned for valuable consideration to
create a work for a film, the person commissioning the work (the
producer) is the absolute first owner of the copyright, entirely
extinguishing the composer's independent rights regarding that specific
film.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the film producers (EIMPA),
holding that composers lose their right to demand royalties for the
public exhibition of the film.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court delivered a defining judgment on the hierarchy of
copyrights in movies. Justice Krishna Iyer held that a cinematograph film
is a composite artwork. When a composer creates music specifically to be
synchronized into a film under a contract of service or for valuable
consideration, the producer becomes the first statutory owner of the
copyright of the film as a whole. This complete ownership subsumes the
underlying musical rights insofar as they relate to the exhibition of the
film. The composer cannot claim a separate royalty when the film is
played in a cinema. (However, the Court noted the composer retains the
right to exploit the music separately from the film, such as selling
audio records).
cases.legalPrinciples:
Ownership in Composite Works: In the absence of a contract to the
contrary, the producer of a cinematograph film is the first owner of the
copyright, defeating the claims of underlying lyricists and composers
regarding the film's public exhibition. (Note: The 2012 Copyright
Amendments drastically changed this rule, legally guaranteeing authors an
unassignable right to receive royalties).

cases.title: Cadila Health Care Ltd. v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd.
cases.facts:
Following a corporate restructuring, the original Cadila group split into
two distinct companies: Cadila Health Care and Cadila Pharmaceuticals.
Cadila Health Care manufactured a drug for treating cerebral malaria
under the brand name "FALCIGO." Shortly after, Cadila Pharmaceuticals
launched a drug for treating the exact same disease under the brand name
"FALCITAB." Both drugs contained the same active ingredient (mefloquine).
Cadila Health Care sued for passing off, arguing the names were
deceptively similar and would cause fatal confusion in the medical
market.
cases.issues:
What is the legal standard for determining "deceptive similarity" and
"passing off" in unregistered trademarks?

Should the threshold for likelihood of confusion be lower or higher for
Schedule H (prescription-only) pharmaceutical products?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Cadila Health Care)
The appellant argued that FALCIGO and FALCITAB are phonetically and
visually identical. Both drugs treat the same severe disease. They argued
that a mix-up in pharmacies could lead to incorrect dosages or
treatments, resulting in fatal consequences.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Cadila Pharmaceuticals)
The respondent argued that "Falci" is a generic prefix derived from the
disease Falciparum malaria, and no one can monopolize it. Furthermore,
they argued that since both drugs are Schedule H prescription medicines,
they are only sold to highly trained pharmacists and doctors, eliminating
any risk of confusion among lay consumers.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Cadila Health Care, laying
down strict, mandatory guidelines for pharmaceutical trademark
infringement.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court flatly rejected the defense that prescription drugs are
immune from confusion. The Court observed the ground reality of India:
prescriptions are often handwritten illegibly, English is not the first
language of many dispensing chemists, and there are varied levels of
infrastructure in rural pharmacies. In this context, relying on the
"sophistication" of doctors is insufficient. The Court established that
in pharmaceutical passing off, the standard of care must be exceptionally
high because a mistake could cost a life. The phonetic similarity between
FALCIGO and FALCITAB was too close for comfort given they treated the
same disease.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Strict Scrutiny for Pharma Marks: The Supreme Court established an
absolute rule that confusing similarity in pharmaceutical trademarks must
be judged with much stricter scrutiny than ordinary consumer goods,
prioritizing public health over trademark defenses.

Rejection of the "Prescription Defense": The fact that a drug is sold
only via prescription does not negate the likelihood of confusion in
trademark infringement/passing off analysis.

cases.title: Reckitt & Colman Products Ltd. v. Borden Inc.
cases.facts:
Reckitt & Colman (the plaintiffs) manufactured and sold lemon juice in
plastic squeeze containers that were designed to exactly mimic the shape,
size, and color of a real lemon. They sold this under the brand name
"Jif." The product became massively popular in the UK. Borden Inc. (the
defendants) decided to enter the market and also began selling their
lemon juice in identical, lemon-shaped plastic containers. Reckitt &
Colman sued for passing off, claiming the specific shape of the lemon
container was their exclusive trade dress.
cases.issues:
Can the shape and physical appearance of a container (trade dress)
function as an unregistered trademark?

What are the essential elements required to successfully prove the common
law tort of passing off?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Reckitt & Colman)
The plaintiffs argued that over decades of exclusive use, the plastic
lemon shape had acquired immense secondary meaning. When consumers saw a
plastic lemon in a supermarket, they didn't just see a container; they
recognized it as the "Jif" brand. Borden's exact copying was a deliberate
attempt to deceive shoppers into buying their product by mistake.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Borden Inc.)
Borden argued that a lemon shape is entirely generic and functional for
selling lemon juice. They argued you cannot monopolize a natural shape.
They also placed small labels with their own name on the lemons, arguing
this was sufficient to distinguish their product from Jif.
cases.judgment:
The UK House of Lords ruled in favor of Reckitt & Colman, granting an
injunction against Borden based on passing off.
cases.reasoning:
Lord Oliver delivered one of the most foundational judgments in trademark
law, establishing the "Classic Trinity" test for passing off. To win, a
plaintiff must prove three elements:

Goodwill: The plaintiff's goods have acquired a reputation in the market
associated with their specific get-up (the plastic lemon).

Misrepresentation: The defendant, intentionally or not, led the public to
believe their goods were the goods of the plaintiff.

Damage: The plaintiff suffered, or is likely to suffer, financial damage
due to this erroneous belief.
The Court found that the Jif lemon had acquired absolute secondary
meaning. Shoppers reached for the shape, rarely reading the small label.
Therefore, Borden's generic labels were insufficient to cure the massive
misrepresentation created by copying the iconic shape.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Classic Trinity of Passing Off: Goodwill, Misrepresentation, and
Damage form the absolute legal threshold for the common law action of
passing off.

Protection of Trade Dress: The physical shape, packaging, and "get-up" of
a product can be protected under passing off if it has acquired
distinctiveness and secondary meaning.

cases.title: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha v. Prius Auto Industries
cases.facts:
Toyota, the global automobile giant, launched the world's first mass-
produced hybrid car, the "Prius," in 1997 in Japan and subsequently
globally, launching it in India much later in 2010. Meanwhile, in 2001,
an Indian auto-parts manufacturer registered the trademark "PRIUS" in
India and began selling spare parts under that name. Toyota sued the
Indian company for trademark infringement and passing off, relying
heavily on the "trans-border reputation" of the Prius brand prior to
2001.
cases.issues:
What evidentiary standard is required to prove "trans-border reputation"
in India?

Does global fame automatically translate to local goodwill necessary to
sustain an action for passing off?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Toyota)
Toyota argued that "Prius" was a revolutionary, globally famous brand. By
2001, it had been heavily featured in international media, automobile
magazines, and the internet. They argued this generated massive trans-
border reputation, making the Indian company's registration of "PRIUS" a
bad-faith hijacking of their intellectual property.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Prius Auto Industries)
The Indian company argued strict territoriality. In 2001, the internet
was not widely used in India, and Toyota had not sold a single Prius in
the country. Therefore, Toyota had no actual goodwill among Indian
consumers. As the honest prior users in the Indian territorial market,
they claimed the rightful ownership of the mark.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the Indian company, Prius
Auto Industries, dismissing Toyota's claim of passing off.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court significantly tightened the doctrine of trans-border
reputation (established in Whirlpool). The Court ruled that trademark
rights are fundamentally territorial. While global reputation exists, a
plaintiff cannot win a passing-off suit merely by proving they are famous
abroad. The plaintiff must provide hard, empirical evidence that their
international reputation had actively "spilled over" into the Indian
market before the defendant adopted the mark. Looking at the evidence
from 2001, the Court found that knowledge of the Prius hybrid car was
restricted to a tiny fraction of automobile enthusiasts and had not
acquired substantial goodwill amongst the general Indian consuming
public. Without actual local goodwill, there can be no passing off.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Territoriality Principle Over Global Fame: In passing off, goodwill
is strictly territorial. Global reputation does not automatically grant
trademark rights in India; a plaintiff must prove actual "spillover" of
that reputation into the specific local jurisdiction prior to the
defendant's use.

cases.title: Hawkins Cookers Ltd. v. Murugan Enterprises
cases.facts:
Hawkins Cookers Ltd. is a famous Indian manufacturer of pressure cookers
and owns the registered trademark "Hawkins." Murugan Enterprises
manufactured and sold spare parts (specifically, rubber gaskets) used in
pressure cookers. Murugan packaged their gaskets with the prominent
phrasing: "Suitable for Hawkins Pressure Cookers." Hawkins sued for
trademark infringement, arguing that the prominent use of their brand
name by an unauthorized third party confused consumers into believing the
spare parts were officially manufactured or endorsed by Hawkins.
cases.issues:
Can a manufacturer of spare parts use a registered trademark to indicate
that their parts are compatible with the trademark owner's product?

What constitutes "nominative fair use" under Section 30 of the Trade
Marks Act, 1999?
cases.arguments:
