A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Hawkins Cookers)
Hawkins argued that Murugan was free-riding on their massive brand
equity. By printing "Hawkins" in large, bold letters on the packaging,
Murugan was not just providing technical information; they were using the
trademark as a primary selling tool, creating a false association of
quality and official endorsement (infringement under Section 29).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Murugan Enterprises)
Murugan relied on Section 30(2)(d) of the Act, which protects the use of
a trademark if it is reasonably necessary to indicate the purpose of an
accessory or spare part. They argued that a consumer needs to know which
cooker the gasket fits. Saying "Suitable for Hawkins" is a factual,
descriptive statement, not a trademark infringement.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Hawkins Cookers, finding that
Murugan's specific manner of using the mark constituted infringement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a fine balance between trademark protection and fair
competition. The Court affirmed the legal principle of Nominative Fair
Use: a spare parts manufacturer is legally allowed to use a competitor's
trademark to indicate compatibility. However, this use is strictly
conditional. The use must be honest, purely descriptive, and limited
exclusively to what is reasonably necessary. The Court examined Murugan's
packaging and found that they had printed the word "Hawkins" in a
massive, stylized font, giving it far more prominence than their own
brand name. This crossed the line from "descriptive information" to
"commercial exploitation." Because the usage was designed to draw undue
attention to the Hawkins mark rather than simply inform the consumer, it
lost the protection of fair use.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Limits of Nominative Fair Use: While third parties can use a registered
trademark to indicate compatibility for spare parts, such use must be
strictly proportional and descriptive. Giving undue visual prominence to
the competitor's mark constitutes infringement.

cases.title: Microfibres Inc. v. Girdhar & Co.
cases.facts:
Microfibres Inc., a US company, manufactured upholstery fabrics. They
created highly original artistic paintings and floral designs, which they
then digitally transferred and printed onto mass-produced fabrics.
Girdhar & Co., an Indian competitor, copied these exact floral patterns
and printed them on their own fabrics. Microfibres sued for copyright
infringement, arguing their floral patterns were "original artistic
works" protected under the Copyright Act. Girdhar & Co. argued that since
the designs were used for mass industrial production, they fell under the
Designs Act, and because Microfibres never registered them as designs,
they had no protection at all.
cases.issues:
What is the boundary between an "artistic work" protected by the
Copyright Act and a "design" protected by the Designs Act?

Does Section 15(2) of the Copyright Act extinguish copyright in an
artistic work if it is applied to an article and mass-produced?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Microfibres Inc.)
The plaintiff argued that a painting is an artistic work, enjoying
inherent copyright protection the moment it is created. The mere fact
that the painting is later printed onto fabric does not strip it of its
fundamental artistic copyright. Copyright requires no registration,
unlike design law.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Girdhar & Co.)
The defendants relied on Section 15(2) of the Copyright Act. This section
states that if a design (capable of being registered under the Designs
Act) is NOT registered, its copyright ceases the moment it is applied to
an article and reproduced more than 50 times by an industrial process.
Since Microfibres mass-produced the fabric, their copyright was legally
extinguished.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled in favor of Girdhar & Co.,
dismissing the copyright infringement suit.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly enforced the legislative boundary separating copyright
and industrial design. The Court held that the legislative intent of
Section 15 is to prevent overlapping monopolies. An original painting
enjoys copyright protection for the author's lifetime plus 60 years.
However, if the author decides to commercialize that painting by applying
it as a "design" to a mass-produced industrial article (like fabric,
wallpaper, or toys), they must register it under the Designs Act (which
offers a much shorter monopoly of 10-15 years). Because Microfibres
applied their artistic work to fabric and reproduced it more than 50
times without securing a design registration, Section 15(2) triggered
automatically, legally annihilating their copyright.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Copyright-Design Interface (Section 15): Establishes an absolute rule
against dual protection. If an artistic work is industrially applied to
an article more than 50 times, the creator loses all copyright protection
unless they previously secured a formal registration under the Designs
Act.

cases.title: Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980) (Note: While an American Supreme Court case, it is universally taught in Indian NLUs as the absolute foundation of global biotechnology patent law, directly informing the interpretation of Indian patent scopes).
cases.facts:
Ananda Chakrabarty, a genetic engineer working for General Electric,
developed a genetically modified bacterium (derived from the Pseudomonas
genus). Through genetic manipulation, this new bacterium was capable of
breaking down multiple components of crude oil-a property possessed by no
naturally occurring bacteria. Chakrabarty filed a patent application for
the bacterium, intending it to be used for cleaning up disastrous oil
spills. The US Patent Office rejected the claim for the bacteria itself,
stating that microorganisms are "products of nature" and living things
are fundamentally unpatentable.
cases.issues:
Does a live, human-made, genetically engineered microorganism constitute
a "manufacture" or "composition of matter" qualifying as patentable
subject matter?

Does the fact that an invention is "alive" automatically place it outside
the scope of patent law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Chakrabarty)
Chakrabarty argued that his bacterium was not a "product of nature." It
did not exist anywhere in the natural world until he engineered it in a
laboratory using complex biochemical processes. He created a new
composition of matter with a highly specific industrial utility,
fulfilling all classical criteria for a patent.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Diamond / Patent Office)
The Patent Office argued that Congress never intended for living
organisms to be patented. They argued that "manufacture" historically
applies to inanimate objects, machines, and chemicals. Allowing patents
on life forms opens a massive ethical and legal Pandora's box that should
only be addressed by specific new legislation, not by judicial
interpretation of old patent laws.
cases.judgment:
The United States Supreme Court (in a tight 5-4 decision) ruled in favor
of Chakrabarty, declaring the genetically engineered bacterium
patentable.
cases.reasoning:
Chief Justice Warren Burger delivered a monumental judgment that birthed
the modern biotech industry. The Court looked at the broad statutory
language of the Patent Act, stating that Congress intended statutory
subject matter to "include anything under the sun that is made by man."
The Court distinguished between unpatentable discoveries (like a newly
found wild plant or a new mineral) and patentable inventions. Chakrabarty
did not just discover an unknown natural bacterium; he manufactured a
product of human ingenuity with distinct characteristics. The Court
concluded that the relevant legal distinction is not between "living and
inanimate" things, but between "products of nature" and "human-made
inventions."
cases.legalPrinciples:
Patentability of Life Forms: The foundational global precedent
establishing that living, genetically modified organisms (microorganisms)
are patentable subject matter provided they are the result of human
intervention and do not occur naturally.

cases.title: Time Warner Entertainment Co. v. RPG Netcom
cases.facts:
Time Warner Entertainment (Warner Bros), a massive US film production
company, discovered that RPG Netcom, a cable television provider in
India, was broadcasting its copyrighted movies to Indian subscribers
without obtaining any licenses or permissions. Time Warner filed a suit
in the Delhi High Court for copyright infringement. RPG Netcom raised a
technical defense, arguing that Time Warner, as a foreign corporate
entity whose movies were produced in the United States, did not have
standing to sue for copyright infringement in an Indian court under the
Indian Copyright Act.
cases.issues:
Do foreign works and foreign copyright owners enjoy copyright protection
within the territorial jurisdiction of India?

What is the effect of the International Copyright Order and the Berne
Convention on enforcing foreign copyrights in Indian courts?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Time Warner Entertainment)
Time Warner argued that copyright is international. India and the United
States are both signatories to the Berne Convention for the Protection of
Literary and Artistic Works and the Universal Copyright Convention. Under
the International Copyright Order passed by the Indian government, works
first published in member countries are granted the exact same protection
in India as if they were first published by an Indian citizen.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (RPG Netcom)
RPG Netcom attempted to exploit territorial loopholes. They argued that
the Indian Copyright Act is designed to protect Indian authors. Since the
movies were not registered in India and the plaintiff had no direct
corporate presence, the Indian courts lacked the jurisdiction to enforce
American copyrights.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled decisively in favor of Time Warner
Entertainment, granting an injunction against the cable operator and
affirming the protection of foreign copyrights.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly upheld the principle of National Treatment mandated by
international IP treaties. The Court examined Section 40 of the Indian
Copyright Act, which empowers the Central Government to extend copyright
protection to foreign works. Through the International Copyright Order,
India fulfills its obligations under the Berne Convention. The Court held
that a work created in any Berne Convention member state automatically
enjoys full copyright protection in India, exactly as if it were an
Indian work. There is no requirement for a foreign entity to register its
copyright in India to sue an Indian infringer. The cable operator's
unauthorized broadcast was a clear violation of these protected
international rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Doctrine of National Treatment: Indian copyright law automatically
protects foreign works originating from treaty member countries,
eliminating the need for local registration to enforce IP rights against
domestic piracy.

Enforceability of International Copyrights: Established a clear, robust
mechanism for multinational entertainment companies to enforce their
copyrights directly against local Indian broadcasters and cable
operators.

cases.title: Dr. Aloys Wobben v. Yogesh Mehra
cases.facts:
Dr. Aloys Wobben, the founder of Enercon GmbH, held several Indian
patents related to wind turbine technology. A joint venture dispute arose
with his Indian partners (the Mehras), leading Wobben to file patent
infringement suits in the High Court. In response, the Mehras filed
counter-claims in the High Court seeking the revocation of Wobben's
patents under Section 64 of the Patents Act. Simultaneously, the Mehras
had also filed revocation petitions before the Intellectual Property
Appellate Board (IPAB) under Section 64, and post-grant oppositions
before the Controller of Patents under Section 25(2).
cases.issues:
Can a party simultaneously pursue multiple remedies to invalidate a
patent across different forums (e.g., a counter-claim in the High Court
and a revocation petition before the IPAB)?

Does the institution of a revocation petition before the IPAB bar a
defendant from filing a counter-claim for revocation in an infringement
suit?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Dr. Aloys Wobben)
Wobben argued that the Mehras were abusing the legal process by "forum
shopping." Allowing simultaneous revocation proceedings on the same
grounds before the Controller, the IPAB, and the High Court would lead to
conflicting decisions and parallel litigation harassment.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Yogesh Mehra)
The Mehras relied on a literal interpretation of the Patents Act. They
argued that Section 64 (revocation) and Section 25 (post-grant
opposition) provide independent statutory rights. Furthermore, Section
104 allows a defendant in an infringement suit to automatically file a
counter-claim for revocation, regardless of other pending proceedings.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Dr. Aloys Wobben, holding
that a party cannot simultaneously pursue multiple revocation proceedings
across different forums.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court applied the doctrine of election. The Court harmonized
the overlapping provisions of the Patents Act to prevent legislative
absurdity. The Court held that if "any person interested" files a
revocation petition before the IPAB, they cannot subsequently file a
counter-claim for revocation in an infringement suit on the same patent.
Conversely, if a counter-claim is filed first, a subsequent IPAB petition
is barred. Furthermore, if a post-grant opposition (Section 25) is
pending, neither a revocation petition nor a counter-claim can be filed
until the opposition is decided. You cannot "ride two horses at the same
time."
cases.legalPrinciples:
Doctrine of Election in Patent Revocation: A challenger must elect one
specific statutory route to invalidate a patent. Parallel and
simultaneous proceedings for the revocation of the same patent before the
Controller, IPAB, and High Court are strictly prohibited.

cases.title: Entertainment Network (India) Ltd. (ENIL) v. Super Cassettes Industries Ltd.
cases.facts:
ENIL operated the popular FM radio station "Radio Mirchi." Super
Cassettes Industries (T-Series) owned the copyright to a massive
catalogue of Bollywood music. T-Series and ENIL failed to agree on the
licensing fees for broadcasting T-Series' music. Consequently, T-Series
refused to grant a license. ENIL broadcasted the songs anyway and
subsequently applied to the Copyright Board for a Compulsory License
under Section 31(1)(b) of the Copyright Act, arguing that T-Series was
unreasonably withholding music from the public. T-Series sued ENIL for
copyright infringement.
cases.issues:
Can a compulsory license under Section 31 of the Copyright Act be granted
simply because the copyright owner and the broadcaster cannot agree on
commercial terms?

What constitutes an "unreasonable refusal" to allow the communication of
a work to the public?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (ENIL / Radio Mirchi)
ENIL argued that FM radio serves a vital public interest by disseminating
music. Once a song is published, the copyright owner cannot create an
absolute monopoly by refusing to license it on reasonable terms. Section
31 was explicitly designed to prevent copyright cartels from holding the
public to ransom.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Super Cassettes / T-Series)
T-Series argued that copyright is private property. They were not
withholding the music from the "public"; the music was widely available
on CDs, cassettes, and other radio stations that agreed to their terms.
Section 31 is an expropriatory provision that should only trigger if the
work is completely hidden from the public, not just because a specific
corporate broadcaster refuses to pay market rates.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled that Section 31 compulsory licenses are
valid and necessary, but remanded the specific matter back to the
Copyright Board to determine reasonable royalties.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court struck a balance between private intellectual property
rights and public access. The Court clarified that "public" under Section
31 does not mean the entire population of India; it includes specific
audiences, like FM radio listeners. If a copyright owner refuses to
license a work on reasonable terms, effectively blocking a specific
medium from communicating it, it triggers Section 31. The Court held that
copyright societies cannot act as monopolies to demand exorbitant fees.
Compulsory licensing is a valid statutory mechanism to break deadlocks
and ensure that published works achieve maximum dissemination while
ensuring the owner receives a "reasonable" royalty.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Compulsory Licensing for Broadcasts: Established that broadcasters have a
statutory right to seek a compulsory license if a copyright owner demands
commercially unreasonable terms, ensuring that music remains accessible
to the public via radio.

cases.title: Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson v. Micromax Informatics Ltd.
cases.facts:
Ericsson, a global telecommunications giant, held several Standard
Essential Patents (SEPs) for 2G, 3G, and EDGE mobile technologies. SEPs
are patents that a manufacturer absolutely must use to comply with
international technical standards. Ericsson had committed to licensing
these SEPs on Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory (FRAND) terms.
Ericsson sued Micromax, an Indian mobile brand, for patent infringement,
claiming Micromax refused to sign a FRAND license and was using the
technology for free. Micromax retaliated by complaining to the
Competition Commission of India (CCI), alleging that Ericsson was abusing
its dominant position by demanding excessive, discriminatory royalties
based on the final price of the phone, rather than the value of the
patented chip.
cases.issues:
Can the Competition Commission of India (CCI) investigate a patent holder
for "abuse of dominance" under the Competition Act for the manner in
which they negotiate SEP licenses?

Does the Patents Act comprehensively govern patent licensing, thereby
excluding the jurisdiction of the CCI?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Ericsson)
Ericsson argued that patents grant a statutory monopoly. Any dispute
regarding royalties or compulsory licensing falls exclusively under the
jurisdiction of the Patents Act and the civil courts. They argued that
the CCI had no jurisdiction to interfere in the legitimate exercise of
intellectual property rights, and their royalty demands were standard
global FRAND terms.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Micromax / CCI)
Micromax argued that while the patent itself is legal, the behavior of
the patentee in the market can be anti-competitive. Because Ericsson's
patents were "Essential" (SEPs), they enjoyed an absolute monopoly.
Demanding extortionate royalties under the threat of injunctions
constituted an abuse of dominant position, triggering the jurisdiction of
the Competition Act.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled that the Competition Commission of India (CCI)
does have the jurisdiction to investigate an SEP holder for anti-
competitive practices, allowing the CCI probe to proceed alongside the
patent infringement suit.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on the intersection of IP and
Competition law. The Court held that the Patents Act and the Competition
Act are not mutually exclusive; they must be read harmoniously. While the
Patents Act protects the right of the inventor to exclude others, it does
not grant the inventor a license to abuse that monopoly to distort the
free market. Because SEPs lock entire industries into using specific
patents, the patent holder inherently holds a dominant market position.
If the patentee violates their FRAND commitments by demanding
discriminatory or exorbitant royalties, it constitutes an abuse of
dominance actionable under the Competition Act.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Jurisdiction of Competition Law over IP: Established that the exercise of
intellectual property rights, particularly involving Standard Essential
Patents (SEPs), is subject to antitrust scrutiny by the CCI.

FRAND Obligations: Highlighted the legal enforceability of FRAND
commitments, preventing patent hold-up in standard-setting industries.

cases.title: Ferid Allani v. Union of India
cases.facts:
Ferid Allani filed a patent application in India for a "method and device
for accessing information sources and services on the web." The Indian
Patent Office rejected the application, citing Section 3(k) of the
Patents Act, 1970, which strictly prohibits the patenting of "a
mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or
algorithms." The Controller concluded that since the invention was
implemented through software executing on a generic computer, it was
merely a computer program per se and thus unpatentable. Allani appealed
to the Delhi High Court.
cases.issues:
What is the legal interpretation of the phrase "computer programme per
se" under Section 3(k) of the Patents Act?

Can a software-based invention be patented if it produces a "technical
effect" or solves a technical problem?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Ferid Allani)
Allani argued that his invention was not just raw code (a program per
se). It was a highly structured method that improved the internal
functioning of a device, resulting in faster and more efficient web
access. He argued that if a software program provides a tangible
"technical effect" or a "technical contribution," it escapes the Section
3(k) bar.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Union of India / Patent Office)
The Patent Office relied on a strict, literal interpretation. They argued
that any invention where the novelty lies entirely in the software code,
and which runs on standard, known hardware, is explicitly barred by
Section 3(k) to prevent the monopolization of basic coding logic.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Ferid Allani, setting aside the
Patent Office's rejection and ordering a re-examination of the
application based on the "technical effect" test.
cases.reasoning:
The Court revolutionized the patentability of Computer Related Inventions
(CRIs) in India. The Court held that the addition of the words "per se"
in Section 3(k) was deliberate by the legislature. It means that while
abstract software code itself (like a novel algorithm) cannot be
patented, an invention that uses software to solve a technical problem is
patentable. If a computer program results in a "technical effect" (such
as improving memory efficiency, enhancing processing speed, or securing
data transmission), it transforms from a mere program per se into a
patentable technological invention. Denying patents to all software-
implemented inventions would be catastrophic for modern innovation,
spanning AI, blockchain, and IoT.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The "Technical Effect" Test: Established that software and Computer
Related Inventions (CRIs) are patentable in India despite Section 3(k),
provided the applicant demonstrates that the software produces a concrete
"technical effect" or "technical contribution" to the hardware or
process.

cases.title: Make My Trip (India) Private Limited v. Make My Travel (India) Private Limited
cases.facts:
MakeMyTrip, a massive Indian online travel agency (OTA), owned the
registered trademarks "MakeMyTrip" and its associated logos. The
defendant, a smaller, newer travel agency, began operating under the name
"Make My Travel," using a highly similar color scheme and font for its
logo. MakeMyTrip filed a trademark infringement and passing off suit,
arguing that the defendant intentionally adopted a deceptively similar
mark to confuse consumers in the same service sector.
cases.issues:
Is the phrase "Make My Trip" inherently distinctive, or is it a
descriptive combination of common English words that cannot be
monopolized?

Does the defendant's use of "Make My Travel" constitute deceptive
similarity leading to passing off?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (MakeMyTrip)
The plaintiff argued that while the individual words are common, their
specific combination ("MakeMyTrip") had acquired immense secondary
meaning through billions of rupees in advertising and years of dominant
market presence. They argued that "Make My Travel" was phonetically,
conceptually, and visually identical, clearly designed to free-ride on
their established goodwill.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Make My Travel)
The defendant argued that "Make," "My," and "Trip/Travel" are generic
dictionary words describing the service of travel booking. Nobody can
claim an exclusive monopoly over such descriptive terms. They argued that
consumers booking travel are careful and would not confuse the two
entities.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of MakeMyTrip, granting an absolute
injunction against the defendant's use of the name "Make My Travel."
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that while the words "Make," "My," and "Trip" are ordinary
dictionary words, their specific combination was a coined mark. Even if
considered descriptive, the Court found that MakeMyTrip had submitted
overwhelming evidence of extensive use, advertising, and market
dominance. Consequently, the mark had acquired absolute secondary
meaning, identifying the plaintiff exclusively. The Court applied the
test of the "unwary purchaser of average intelligence and imperfect
recollection." A consumer looking at "Make My Travel" with a similar logo
would almost certainly assume it was affiliated with or a subsidiary of
the famous "MakeMyTrip" brand. The adoption of the mark was clearly
malafide.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Secondary Meaning of Descriptive Marks: A mark composed of generic or
descriptive words can acquire strong trademark protection if the
proprietor proves it has achieved distinct secondary meaning through
extensive commercial use.

Deceptive Conceptual Similarity: Infringement occurs not just through
exact copying, but when a rival adopts a mark that shares the identical
conceptual layout and visual get-up of a famous mark in the same service
sector.

cases.title: Star India Pvt. Ltd. v. Moviestu.be
cases.facts:
Star India acquired the exclusive broadcasting rights for a major
international cricket tournament. Anticipating massive piracy, Star India
filed a civil suit in the Delhi High Court days before the tournament
began. They sued several specific rogue websites (like Moviestu.be) known
for illegally streaming sports content. Crucially, they also sued
internet service providers (ISPs) and sought a "John Doe" (Ashok Kumar)
order-a blanket injunction to block not only the named websites but also
any unnamed, future websites that might pop up to stream the matches
illegally during the tournament.
cases.issues:
Can a court issue a preemptive "John Doe" (Ashok Kumar) injunction
against unknown, anonymous entities to prevent anticipated copyright
infringement?

How can copyright owners combat digital piracy when infringers constantly
change domain names to evade specific blocking orders?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Star India)
Star India argued that sports broadcasting rights are highly perishable;
their value vanishes the moment the live match ends. If they have to file
a new lawsuit every time a pirate site changes its URL, the legal remedy
becomes useless. They needed a dynamic, preemptive order allowing ISPs to
block mirror sites immediately upon notification by the plaintiff.

B. Arguments for the Defendants (ISPs / Amicus Curiae)
ISPs and free speech advocates raised concerns about overly broad
blocking orders. They argued that giving a private broadcaster the power
to mandate website blocking without judicial scrutiny of each specific
URL could lead to the censorship of legitimate, non-infringing websites.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Star India, granting the "John
Doe" (Ashok Kumar) order and formulating the framework for "Dynamic
Injunctions."
cases.reasoning:
The Court recognized the technological reality of internet piracy, where
rogue websites ("hydra-headed monsters") constantly spawn mirror URLs to
bypass static injunctions. To make copyright enforcement effective, the
Court adapted the traditional John Doe jurisprudence into a "Dynamic
Injunction." The Court authorized the ISPs to block the specific rogue
websites named in the suit. Furthermore, the Court permitted the
plaintiff to notify the ISPs of any new mirror/alphanumeric variations of
the blocked sites that appeared during the tournament, and the ISPs were
mandated to block those new URLs immediately without requiring the
plaintiff to return to court for a fresh order.
cases.legalPrinciples:
John Doe (Ashok Kumar) Orders: Affirmed the use of ex-parte injunctions
against unnamed defendants in IP infringement cases.

Dynamic Injunctions: Created a powerful mechanism allowing rights holders
to enforce blocking orders against mirror websites and new domains
dynamically, protecting perishable IP like live sports broadcasts.

cases.title: Crocs Inc. USA v. Bata India Ltd.
cases.facts:
Crocs Inc. was globally famous for its distinctive, perforated, clog-
style plastic footwear. Crocs had registered the shape and configuration
of this footwear as an industrial "design" in India under the Designs
Act. However, the design registration eventually expired. Following the
expiration, Indian footwear companies, including Bata India, began
manufacturing and selling identical clog-style shoes. Since they could no
longer sue for design infringement, Crocs filed a suit for "passing off"
under the Trade Marks Act, arguing that the physical shape of the shoe
had become a well-known trademark (trade dress) and Bata was confusing
consumers.
cases.issues:
Can a product shape that was previously registered as an industrial
design be protected as an unregistered trademark (trade dress) through a
passing-off action once the design patent expires?

Does the expiration of a statutory design monopoly automatically thrust
the shape into the public domain?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Crocs Inc.)
Crocs argued that rights under the Designs Act and the Trade Marks Act
are not mutually exclusive. Even if the design monopoly expired, the
specific shape of the clog had acquired massive secondary meaning over
the years. The public associates that specific shape exclusively with
Crocs. Therefore, Bata copying the shape constituted the tort of passing
off.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Bata India)
Bata relied heavily on the legislative bargain of IP law. They argued
that an industrial design grants a limited statutory monopoly (maximum 15
years). Once that expires, the design falls into the public domain for
all to use. Allowing Crocs to claim trademark rights over the exact same
shape would effectively grant them a perpetual backdoor monopoly,
destroying the purpose of the Designs Act.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled in favor of Bata India,
dismissing Crocs's suit for passing off.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a definitive boundary between design law and trademark
law. The Court held that a registered design cannot inherently constitute
a trademark. The legislative intent of the Designs Act is to reward the
creator with a limited monopoly, after which the public benefits from
free competition. If the shape of the product itself (which was the
registered design) is claimed as a trademark post-expiration, it
illegally extends the monopoly forever. The Court held that a passing off
action for trade dress is only maintainable if the plaintiff can prove
that the distinctive elements they are claiming as a trademark are extra
elements, wholly separate from the features that were registered as the
design. Since Crocs was claiming the entire shoe shape (the expired
design) as the trademark, the claim failed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Design-Trademark Interface: Once an industrial design registration
expires, the shape and configuration of the article fall into the public
domain. The creator cannot use the common law tort of passing off to
claim trademark rights over that exact same shape to secure a perpetual
monopoly.

cases.title: Reckitt Benckiser (India) Ltd. v. Hindustan Unilever Ltd.
cases.facts:
This case is one of the many fierce battles in the "Dettol vs. Lifebuoy"
soap wars. Hindustan Unilever (HUL), the manufacturer of Lifebuoy soap,
aired a television commercial showing a child washing his hands with an
unnamed antiseptic liquid that was visually identical to the famous
Dettol bottle (owned by Reckitt Benckiser). The commercial depicted the
antiseptic liquid as ineffective at killing germs rapidly compared to
Lifebuoy soap. Reckitt Benckiser sued HUL for trade disparagement and
sought an injunction to pull the advertisement off the air.
cases.issues:
What is the legal boundary between permissible comparative advertising
("puffery") and illegal trade disparagement?

Can an advertisement be disparaging even if it does not explicitly name
the competitor's product, but heavily implies it through visual cues?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Reckitt Benckiser)
Reckitt argued that the bottle shown in the ad, while unlabeled, was the
iconic amber liquid in the sword-hilted bottle universally recognized as
Dettol. They argued the ad went beyond claiming Lifebuoy was good; it
actively denigrated Dettol by falsely depicting it as entirely
ineffective at killing germs, damaging Dettol's core brand equity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Hindustan Unilever)
HUL argued the defense of comparative advertising. They claimed they were
simply highlighting the scientifically proven superiority of their soap's
fast-acting formula. They argued they did not name Dettol, and the liquid
shown was a generic representation of all liquid antiseptics.
Furthermore, claiming one's own product is "better" is legally permitted
puffery.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Reckitt Benckiser, granting an
injunction against HUL and ordering the removal of the disparaging
advertisement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the definitive test for trade disparagement in India.
A company is absolutely free to boast that its product is the best in the
world (puffery), and they can even compare their product to a rival to
show why theirs is better. However, a company cannot say that the
competitor's product is bad, useless, or harmful. The Court held that
while HUL didn't name Dettol, the visual representation was unmistakably
Dettol. The advertisement crossed the line from "Lifebuoy is good" to
"Dettol is useless." Because the commercial actively denigrated the
rival's product and portrayed it in a negative light, it constituted
actionable trade disparagement.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Trade Disparagement vs. Puffery: In comparative advertising, you can
declare your goods to be superior, but you cannot denigrate, defame, or
state that a competitor's goods are inferior, ineffective, or harmful.

Implied Identification: Disparagement occurs even without explicitly
naming the rival, provided the visual cues (trade dress, packaging)
clearly identify the targeted brand to the reasonable consumer.

cases.title: Christian Louboutin Sas v. Nakul Bajaj
cases.facts:
Nakul Bajaj operated an e-commerce website called Darveys.com, an
exclusive, members-only platform that sold luxury brands at a discount.
The website featured heavily discounted Christian Louboutin shoes.
Louboutin, which tightly controls its luxury supply chain and had not
authorized Darveys to sell its products, sued for trademark infringement.
They alleged that Darveys was selling counterfeit shoes or parallel
imports that damaged the brand. Darveys claimed immunity under Section 79
of the Information Technology (IT) Act, arguing it was merely an
"intermediary" connecting buyers and independent sellers.
cases.issues:
Under what circumstances can an e-commerce platform claim "safe harbor"
immunity as an intermediary under Section 79 of the IT Act in cases of
trademark infringement?

What is the legal distinction between an "active" and a "passive" e-
commerce intermediary?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Christian Louboutin)
Louboutin argued that Darveys was not a neutral platform like an internet
service provider. Darveys actively curated the products, guaranteed their
authenticity, handled the shipping, and dictated the prices. Because
Darveys was actively involved in the commercial transaction and promotion
of the infringing goods, they could not hide behind the intermediary safe
harbor.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Nakul Bajaj / Darveys)
The defendant argued that the actual sellers were independent boutiques
listed on the site. Darveys merely provided the technology platform for
these third-party sellers to meet buyers. They relied on Section 79,
stating they should only be liable if they refused to take down a
specific listing after receiving actual knowledge of infringement.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Christian Louboutin, declaring
that Darveys.com was an "active" participant and therefore not entitled
to the intermediary safe harbor.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Pratibha M. Singh delivered a highly nuanced judgment defining
the liabilities of modern e-commerce platforms. The Court differentiated
between "passive" intermediaries (who merely provide access/hosting) and
"active" participants. The Court listed several factors that destroy safe
harbor immunity: if the platform provides authenticity guarantees,
handles warehousing and logistics, actively curates the sellers, uses the
trademark to promote the platform, or directly benefits from the sale of
the infringing goods. Because Darveys controlled almost every aspect of
the transaction except manufacturing the shoe, they were an active
participant in the commercial supply chain. Therefore, they were strictly
liable for trademark infringement and passing off, stripped of Section 79
protection.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Active vs. Passive Intermediaries: E-commerce platforms that actively
manage logistics, guarantee authenticity, and curate product listings are
"active participants" in the sale and forfeit the safe harbor protection
granted to passive intermediaries under the IT Act.

E-commerce Trademark Liability: Marketplaces that actively use luxury
trademarks to draw traffic and facilitate unauthorized sales can be held
directly liable for trademark infringement.

cases.title: D.M. Entertainment Pvt. Ltd. v. Baby Gift House
cases.facts:
D.M. Entertainment, an event management company, held the exclusive
rights to manage the commercial interests and intellectual property of
Daler Mehndi, a massively famous Indian pop singer known for his unique
appearance, dancing style, and vocal delivery. The defendants (Baby Gift
House and others) began manufacturing and selling small, musical plastic
dolls. These dolls were visual caricatures of Daler Mehndi and, when
wound up, played brief snippets of his most famous songs. D.M.
Entertainment sued the toy sellers, claiming infringement of Daler
Mehndi's right of publicity and passing off.
cases.issues:
Does Indian law recognize the "Right of Publicity" as a distinct legal
right protectable under the tort of passing off?

Can a celebrity prevent the unauthorized commercial exploitation of their
persona, likeness, and identity by a third party selling merchandise?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (D.M. Entertainment)
The plaintiff argued that Daler Mehndi's persona, image, and voice
possessed massive commercial value (goodwill). By creating dolls that
looked and sounded exactly like him without authorization, the defendants
were commercially exploiting his identity for profit. This constituted
false endorsement and passing off, confusing consumers into believing the
singer had authorized the toys.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Baby Gift House)
The defendants argued that a person's image or likeness is not a
registered trademark. They contended that selling novelty caricature
dolls did not imply any official endorsement by the singer, and there was
no specific statutory law in India explicitly granting a "right of
publicity."
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of D.M. Entertainment, recognizing
the Right of Publicity and granting an injunction against the sale of the
unauthorized dolls.
cases.reasoning:
The Delhi High Court officially cemented the Right of Publicity in Indian
IP jurisprudence. The Court held that the right of publicity evolves from
the right to privacy and is the inherent right of an individual to
control the commercial exploitation of their name, image, likeness, or
persona. For a celebrity, this persona translates into immense commercial
goodwill. The Court applied the classical tort of passing off to this
concept. By selling dolls that unmistakably replicated Daler Mehndi's
physical appearance and voice, the defendants were misappropriating his
goodwill for their own financial gain. The public would naturally assume
the celebrity had authorized or endorsed the merchandise. Therefore, the
unauthorized commercial use of a celebrity's identity constitutes an
actionable wrong.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Right of Publicity: An individual (particularly a celebrity) has the
exclusive right to control the commercial exploitation of their identity,
likeness, and persona.

Passing off of Persona: The unauthorized use of a celebrity's identity to
sell merchandise constitutes the tort of passing off, as it
misappropriates the celebrity's goodwill and falsely implies their
endorsement.

cases.title: Hindustan Pencils Pvt. Ltd. v. India Stationery Products Co.
cases.facts:
Hindustan Pencils manufactured the highly popular "Nataraj" pencils,
holding registered trademarks for the name and the distinct red-and-black
color scheme with specific geometric patterns. India Stationery Products
began manufacturing identical pencils using the name "Nataraj" and
directly copied the packaging and color scheme. Hindustan Pencils sued
for trademark infringement and passing off. The defendants raised a
primary defense of "delay and laches," arguing that Hindustan Pencils had
known about the infringement for years but did nothing, effectively
acquiescing to the defendant's use of the mark.
cases.issues:
Does a delay in filing an infringement suit (laches) automatically defeat
a registered trademark owner's right to an interim injunction?

What is the legal distinction between mere delay and active
"acquiescence" in intellectual property law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Hindustan Pencils)
The plaintiff argued that trademark infringement is a continuing wrong.
Every new pencil sold is a fresh infringement. They argued that unless
the defendant can prove the plaintiff actively encouraged the
infringement, mere delay in approaching the court should not serve as a
shield for a blatant, bad-faith counterfeiter.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (India Stationery Products)
The defendants argued the equitable doctrine of laches. They claimed they
had invested heavily in building their business over the years while the
plaintiff stood by and watched silently. Granting an injunction now would
unjustly destroy their established business.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Hindustan Pencils, rejecting the
defense of delay and granting the interim injunction against the
counterfeiters.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on the intersection of equity and
statutory rights. The Court held that in cases of deliberate, bad-faith
counterfeiting, "delay" by itself is not a valid defense to an
injunction. If the defendant knowingly stole a famous mark, they did so
at their own peril. The Court distinguished delay from "acquiescence."
Acquiescence requires the plaintiff to actively encourage or misleadingly
permit the defendant to build their business. Mere silence or taking time
to file a suit is not acquiescence. Furthermore, the Court noted that
trademark law protects the consumer as much as the proprietor; allowing a
counterfeiter to continue selling fake goods just because the plaintiff
was slow to sue would perpetrate a fraud on the general public.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Delay vs. Acquiescence: Mere delay in bringing a trademark infringement
suit will not defeat an injunction if the adoption of the mark was
dishonest and fraudulent. Injunctions will only be denied if there is
positive, active acquiescence by the rights holder.

Public Interest in Counterfeiting: Courts prioritize the protection of
the consumer from deceptive goods over the equitable defenses (like
laches) claimed by a bad-faith infringer.

cases.title: Nandhini Deluxe v. Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers Federation Ltd.
cases.facts:
The Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) was a massive state cooperative that
sold milk and dairy products under the registered trademark "NANDINI."
Years later, a restaurant chain in Karnataka began operating under the
name "NANDHINI DELUXE," selling meat-heavy Andhra-style cuisine. When the
restaurant applied to register its trademark, KMF opposed it, arguing
that "NANDINI" was a household name in Karnataka and the restaurant's use
of the phonetically identical mark would cause massive consumer confusion
and dilute KMF's brand.
cases.issues:
Can a trademark proprietor claim an absolute monopoly over a mark across
entirely different classes of goods and services?

Does the use of a common/descriptive word as a trademark limit the scope
of protection against dissimilar goods?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Nandhini Deluxe / Restaurant)
The restaurant argued that "Nandini" is a highly common Indian name and
the name of a mythological cow; it is not a coined or inherently
distinctive word. Furthermore, they operated in an entirely different
class (restaurants/meat vs. packaged dairy). No reasonable consumer would
walk into a non-vegetarian restaurant and assume it was run by the state
milk cooperative.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (KMF)
KMF argued that their mark was universally famous in Karnataka. They
argued that food services (restaurants) and food products (milk) are
allied/cognate goods. The phonetic similarity was absolute, and consumers
would inevitably assume the restaurant was an extension of the famous
dairy brand.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Nandhini Deluxe, allowing
the restaurant to register and use its trademark.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court strictly applied the classification of goods under the
Trade Marks Act. The Court held that a proprietor does not get a blanket
monopoly over a word across all 45 classes of goods and services unless
it is a highly distinct, coined word with massive trans-class reputation
(like "Kodak"). Because "Nandini" is a common word, its protection is
narrow. The Court found that milk/dairy and running a restaurant are
distinct trades. The visual representation of the marks was entirely
different (KMF used a cow logo, the restaurant used a lamp).
Consequently, there was absolutely no likelihood of confusion or
deception among the purchasing public.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Limits of Common Word Marks: Trademarks derived from common dictionary
words or generic names receive narrower protection, restricting the
proprietor's ability to block the mark's use in unrelated classes of
goods.

Dissimilar Goods Doctrine: Infringement requires a likelihood of
confusion. Using an identical mark for entirely dissimilar and unrelated
goods/services does not constitute infringement.

cases.title: Garware Plastics & Polyester Ltd. v. Telelink
cases.facts:
Garware Plastics owned the exclusive video rights to several
cinematograph films. They discovered that Telelink, a private cable
operator, was playing videotapes of these films in a central control room
and transmitting them via closed-circuit cable to the television sets of
various paying subscribers living in an apartment complex. Garware sued
for copyright infringement, arguing that this transmission constituted an
unauthorized "communication to the public." Telelink argued they were
merely facilitating private viewing inside private homes, not running a
public cinema.
cases.issues:
What constitutes "communication to the public" under the Copyright Act,
1957?

Does transmitting a film via cable to the private living rooms of
multiple individual subscribers transform a private viewing into a public
exhibition?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Garware Plastics)
Garware argued that the definition of "public" is not restricted to
people gathered in a single public hall. The subscribers to the cable
service were a segment of the public who paid a fee for the transmission.
Therefore, broadcasting the copyright-protected tape to them was a
commercial, public exhibition violating the owner's exclusive rights.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Telelink)
Telelink argued that a person watching television in the privacy of their
own bedroom is the absolute opposite of "public." They argued the cable
simply replaced the individual buying a tape and playing it on their own
VCR, which is a legal private use.
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court ruled in favor of Garware Plastics, holding that
the cable transmission constituted an illegal communication to the
public.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment interpreting technological
transmission under copyright law. The Court held that the test for
"communication to the public" does not depend on where the audience is
physically located (e.g., in a cinema vs. in a bedroom). The crucial test
is the nature of the audience. The cable operator was offering a
commercial service to any resident willing to pay. The subscribers were
united not by a domestic or private family bond, but by their commercial
relationship with the cable provider. Therefore, transmitting the film to
this paying segment of the community constituted a communication to the
public, requiring a license from the copyright owner.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Definition of "Public" in Broadcasting: "Public" under copyright law
includes any targeted, paying audience or segment of the community,
regardless of whether they view the copyrighted work in a public square
or the privacy of their own homes.

Cable Piracy: Established the foundational legal framework that
unauthorized cable and network transmissions of films infringe the
exclusive right of communication to the public.

cases.title: Warner Bros. Entertainment Inc. v. Harinder Kohli
cases.facts:
Warner Bros. owns the global trademark and copyrights for the massive
"Harry Potter" franchise. Harinder Kohli, an Indian film producer,
decided to release a Punjabi comedy film titled Hari Puttar: A Comedy of
Terrors. The film was about a young Indian boy named Hari Prasad Dhoonda
(nicknamed Hari Puttar) who is left home alone and fights off burglars.
Warner Bros. sued for trademark infringement and passing off, arguing
that "Hari Puttar" was deceptively, phonetically similar to "Harry
Potter" and intended to free-ride on their global reputation.
cases.issues:
Does phonetic similarity between a global trademark and a localized,
culturally distinct title constitute trademark infringement?

Is the target audience's sophistication relevant in determining the
likelihood of confusion between a serious fantasy franchise and a local
comedy?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Warner Bros.)
Warner Bros. argued that "Harry Potter" is a well-known mark with immense
trans-border reputation. They contended that "Hari Puttar" sounds almost
identical. They argued that consumers might mistakenly believe the
Punjabi movie was an authorized spoof, a localized spin-off, or somehow
officially connected to the Harry Potter franchise, thereby diluting
their brand.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Harinder Kohli)
The defendant argued that "Hari" is one of the most common names in
India, and "Puttar" means "son" in Punjabi. It is a common term of
endearment. Furthermore, the storylines had absolutely zero overlap (the
Indian movie was a rip-off of Home Alone, not Harry Potter). They argued
no Indian consumer would ever confuse a Punjabi comedy about a boy in a
house with a multi-million dollar Hollywood wizard fantasy.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Harinder Kohli, dismissing Warner
Bros.' application for an interim injunction and allowing the film to be
released.
cases.reasoning:
The Court focused on the socio-cultural context of the target audience.
The Court noted that the audience for Harry Potter consists of literate,
urban consumers who read English books and watch Hollywood movies. This
specific demographic is highly sophisticated and perfectly capable of
distinguishing between a global wizarding franchise and a localized
Punjabi comedy. "Hari" and "Puttar" are culturally ubiquitous terms in
India. Given the total dissimilarity in the products (fantasy vs.
slapstick comedy) and the sophistication of the consumer base, the Court
found there was absolutely no likelihood of cognitive confusion or
deception.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Target Audience Test: In passing off and infringement, phonetic
similarity is not judged in a vacuum. Courts must analyze the specific
demographic that consumes the products; highly sophisticated consumers
are less likely to be confused by phonetic puns.

Cultural Context of Marks: Global trademarks cannot be used to monopolize
common, everyday cultural or linguistic phrases in local jurisdictions
unless there is actual proof of deceptive intent and consumer confusion.

cases.title: Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Glenmark Pharmaceuticals Ltd.
cases.facts:
Merck held an Indian patent for Sitagliptin, a highly successful anti-
diabetic drug (marketed as Januvia). Merck licensed the drug to another
company to sell in India. Glenmark Pharmaceuticals, an Indian generic
manufacturer, launched generic versions of Sitagliptin (Zita and Zita-
Met) at a lower price. Merck sued for patent infringement and sought an
interim injunction. Glenmark argued the patent was invalid for lacking an
inventive step, and furthermore, that Merck's basic patent only covered
the base molecule, while Glenmark was using a specific "salt" of
Sitagliptin that wasn't explicitly disclosed in the primary patent
claims.
cases.issues:
Does manufacturing a specific salt/derivative of a patented base molecule
constitute infringement of the original patent?

How should courts apply the principles of interim injunctions in
pharmaceutical patent cases involving drugs for chronic lifestyle
diseases (like diabetes) versus life-threatening acute diseases (like
cancer)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Merck)
Merck argued they invented the base molecule, Sitagliptin. Any salt or
derivative of this molecule inherently utilizes their core invention.
They had priced the drug affordably for the Indian market and ran patient
assistance programs. Allowing a generic to infringe would destroy their
statutory monopoly and discourage research.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Glenmark)
Glenmark argued that the specific salt they used (Sitagliptin Phosphate)
was a separate chemical entity not explicitly claimed in Merck's core
patent. They also relied on the Roche v. Cipla public interest argument,
claiming diabetes is a massive epidemic in India, and an injunction would
deprive millions of cheaper medication.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (and later the Supreme Court) ruled in favor of
Merck, granting an injunction restraining Glenmark from manufacturing and
selling the generic drug.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly upheld the patentee's rights. First, on the technical
front, the Court ruled that if a generic drug relies on the active
therapeutic core of a patented molecule, minor chemical variations (like
using a different salt) do not avoid infringement. Second, the Court
distinguished this case from Roche v. Cipla. While cancer drugs in Roche
had a price gap of lakhs of rupees, the price gap between Merck's
Sitagliptin and Glenmark's generic was relatively marginal. Furthermore,
diabetes is not a sudden, terminal disease where a slight price
difference means immediate death; there were dozens of other cheap, non-
infringing diabetes drugs available on the market. Therefore, the "public
interest" defense could not be used as a blanket shield for blatant
patent infringement when the price disparity wasn't catastrophic.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Scope of Base Molecule Patents: Infringement cannot be evaded merely by
creating chemical salts or derivatives that rely entirely on the
therapeutic efficacy of the patented base molecule.

Limits of the Public Interest Defense: The public health exception for
denying injunctions is not absolute. It requires a catastrophic price
difference and a lack of alternative market treatments; it cannot be
invoked routinely to protect generics from standard patent enforcement.

cases.title: Micolube India Ltd. v. Rakesh Kumar
cases.facts:
The plaintiff had registered the shape of an oil container as an
industrial design under the Designs Act. The defendant began using a
confusingly similar container shape to sell their own oil. Because the
plaintiff had not registered the shape as a trademark, they could not sue
for trademark infringement. Instead, they sued for the common law tort of
"passing off," arguing that the specific shape of the container (the
registered design) had acquired trade dress reputation. The defendant
argued that under the Designs Act, a registered design cannot be a
trademark, and therefore, passing off is not a maintainable remedy for a
design.
cases.issues:
Can a plaintiff simultaneously hold statutory rights under the Designs
Act and common law rights under the tort of passing off for the exact
same physical shape?

Does registering an article as an industrial design legally bar the
proprietor from claiming it functions as a trademark (trade dress)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Micolube India)
The plaintiff argued that design rights and passing off serve different
purposes. Design law protects the aesthetic novelty, while passing off
protects the commercial goodwill and prevents consumer deception. Even if
a design is registered, if it becomes so famous that it identifies the
source of the goods, equity demands that competitors be stopped from
deceiving the public.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Rakesh Kumar)
The defendant relied strictly on the definitions within the statutes. The
Designs Act explicitly excludes any shape that functions as a trademark.
Therefore, the moment the plaintiff registered it as a design, they
legally conceded it was not a trademark. To allow a passing off suit
would blur the lines and grant a perpetual trademark monopoly to an
expiring design.
cases.judgment:
A Full Bench (three judges) of the Delhi High Court ruled that a suit for
passing off is maintainable with respect to an article registered as a
design, provided specific conditions are met.
cases.reasoning:
The Full Bench resolved a massive conflict in Indian IP jurisprudence.
The Court held that the rights are fundamentally different. Design
registration is a statutory monopoly; passing off is a common law remedy
against fraud. The Court ruled that the statutory exclusion (that a
design cannot be a trademark) applies at the time of registration.
However, after a novel design is registered and put into the market, it
is perfectly possible that over time, the public begins to associate that
specific aesthetic shape with the manufacturer. If the shape acquires
"secondary meaning," the proprietor can launch a passing off action.
However, the plaintiff must prove that the passing off is based on
elements of trade dress that are larger or different from the mere
aesthetic novelty that was registered as the design.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Co-existence of Rights: The registration of an industrial design does not
completely extinguish the common law remedy of passing off.

Post-Registration Secondary Meaning: If a registered design acquires
distinct secondary meaning and functions as a source identifier in
commerce, the proprietor can protect it via passing off, provided they
prove consumer deception beyond mere design copying.

cases.title: Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation Ltd. (Amul) v. Hindustan Unilever Ltd.
cases.facts:
GCMMF, the makers of "Amul" ice cream, launched a massive television
advertising campaign. The commercial urged consumers to eat "real" ice
cream made from pure milk (showing a cup of milk) and warned them against
eating "frozen desserts" made from vanaspati (hydrogenated vegetable
oil), depicting the oil flowing into a cup in a highly unappetizing
manner. Hindustan Unilever (HUL), the market leader in frozen desserts
(under the Kwality Wall's brand), sued Amul for trade disparagement. HUL
argued that their frozen desserts were made from edible vegetable oil,
not the unhealthy vanaspati depicted in the ad.
cases.issues:
Does generic disparagement (attacking an entire category of goods)
constitute actionable trade disparagement, even if no specific
competitor's brand is named?

Is an advertisement disparaging if it uses factually incorrect scientific
representations to create a negative psychological impact?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Hindustan Unilever)
HUL argued that because they held the dominant market share in frozen
desserts, an attack on the entire category was directly an attack on
Kwality Wall's. They proved that practically no major frozen dessert in
India used vanaspati (which implies unhealthy trans-fats); they used
healthy edible vegetable oils. Amul's visual depiction was a deliberate,
scientific lie designed to create disgust and fear among parents,
illegally disparaging HUL's products.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Amul)
Amul argued that the advertisement was an educational campaign based on
truth. By law, products made with vegetable oil cannot be called "ice
cream"; they must be labeled "frozen dessert." Amul claimed they were
merely informing the consumer to read the label. They argued they did not
name HUL, and educating the public about product categories is a
protected right of commercial speech.
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court ruled in favor of Hindustan Unilever, granting an
injunction against Amul and ordering the removal of the disparaging
advertisement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reinforced the boundaries of comparative advertising. First,
the Court held that generic disparagement is actionable. If a plaintiff
commands a massive share of a specific market category, denigrating that
entire category causes direct financial damage to the plaintiff, even if
their brand is not named. Second, while Amul was legally correct that
frozen desserts use vegetable oil, their visual representation of
vanaspati/dalda (associated with cheap, unhealthy, solid fats) was
factually false and maliciously misleading. The purpose of the ad was not
to educate, but to instill revulsion. You can legally say "my milk ice
cream is better than vegetable oil dessert," but you cannot lie to the
public to make the competitor's product look toxic.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Generic Disparagement Actionability: A company can sue for trade
disparagement if an advertisement attacks an entire class of goods,
provided the company is a leading manufacturer of that specific class.

Visual Misrepresentation: Creating consumer fear or disgust through
factually incorrect visual implications about a rival's ingredients
crosses the line from puffery into illegal disparagement.

cases.title: Najma Heptulla v. Orient Longman Ltd.
cases.facts:
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, a prominent Indian freedom fighter, dictated his
memoirs to Humayun Kabir in Urdu. Kabir translated and drafted the book
in English, titled India Wins Freedom. Both men agreed that thirty pages
of the manuscript, containing highly sensitive political opinions, would
remain sealed in the National Archives and not be published until 30
years after Azad's death. When the 30 years expired, Azad's legal heirs
(including Najma Heptulla) sued the publishers (Orient Longman) to stop
the publication of the 30 pages. They claimed that Azad was the sole
author, and they, as his heirs, owned the copyright and had the right to
prevent publication.
cases.issues:
What constitutes "joint authorship" under the Copyright Act, 1957?

Can the person who physically writes/translates the manuscript claim
joint authorship if the original ideas and dictation came from someone
else?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Najma Heptulla / Heirs)
The plaintiffs argued that Humayun Kabir was merely a scribe or a
translator. The ideas, the history, and the voice were entirely Maulana
Azad's. Since copyright protects the author of the work, Azad was the
sole author. As his legal heirs, they claimed the absolute right to
decide whether the unpublished 30 pages should see the light of day.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Orient Longman / Kabir's Heirs)
The defendants argued that copyright does not protect ideas; it protects
the expression of ideas. Azad did not write the English text; Kabir did.
Kabir took Azad's raw dictation and used his own literary skill and
judgment to craft the English prose. Therefore, they were joint authors
who collaborated on a single, inseparable work, and the original
publication agreement signed by both men was legally binding.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of the publishers, recognizing joint
authorship and allowing the publication of the sealed 30 pages.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic ruling on the idea-expression dichotomy
regarding authorship. The Court examined the prefaces and the working
relationship between Azad and Kabir. The Court held that a person who
merely acts as a stenographer typing out exact words is not an author.
However, Kabir did much more. He listened to Azad in Urdu, translated the
concepts, structured the narrative, and physically authored the English
expression. Because copyright protects the literary expression, Kabir's
contribution of skill and labor made him an author. Since the
contributions of Azad (the ideas/approval) and Kabir (the English
expression) were inseparable, they were "joint authors." Consequently,
the original contract signed by the joint authors to publish the pages
after 30 years was valid and binding, defeating the heirs' attempt to
suppress the text.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Joint Authorship Threshold: A person who takes dictation or ideas and
actively translates, structures, and expresses them in a new literary
form (with the approval of the originator) is a joint author, not a mere
scribe.

Indivisibility of Joint Works: In a work of joint authorship, the rights
are intertwined, and the mutually agreed-upon publishing contracts of the
original authors bind their respective legal heirs.

cases.title: Cluett Peabody & Co. Inc. v. Arrow Apparels
cases.facts:
Cluett Peabody, a US company, owned the globally famous trademark "ARROW"
for men's shirts and collars. They registered the mark in India in the
1950s. Due to strict Indian import restrictions during that era, they
could not physically sell ARROW shirts in India for over 30 years. Arrow
Apparels, an Indian company, began manufacturing and selling shirts in
India under the identical "ARROW" trademark. When Cluett Peabody finally
re-entered the Indian market, they sued for trademark infringement. Arrow
Apparels filed for rectification to remove the American company's mark
from the register on the grounds of "non-use" and "abandonment."
cases.issues:
Does the failure to use a registered trademark in India for over three
decades automatically result in its "abandonment" and removal from the
register?

Does the existence of severe government import restrictions constitute
"special circumstances" excusing the non-use of a trademark?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Cluett Peabody)
The American company argued that they never intended to abandon the mark.
Their absence from the Indian market was entirely involuntary, caused by
draconian Indian import policies and high tariffs that made business
impossible. They argued that "abandonment" requires a voluntary intent to
surrender the mark, which was absent here.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Arrow Apparels)
The Indian company argued the strict statutory rule of "Use it or Lose
it." Section 47 of the Trade Marks Act allows removal if a mark is not
used for five continuous years. They argued 30 years of non-use destroys
any local goodwill. They had built up the Arrow brand in India entirely
through their own labor, and the US company should not be allowed to
resurrect a dead registration.
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court ruled in favor of Cluett Peabody, protecting their
trademark and rejecting the claim of abandonment.
cases.reasoning:
The Court protected the rights of international brand owners navigating
restrictive trade regimes. The Court held that "abandonment" requires
both non-use and an intention to abandon. The Court noted that Cluett
Peabody had fiercely protected its mark globally and had continued to
renew its Indian registration throughout the 30 years, proving an intent
to keep the rights alive. Furthermore, the Court recognized the "special
circumstances in the trade" exception. The absolute ban on importing
foreign garments into India was a government-imposed impossibility, not a
voluntary business choice. Since the non-use was due to external special
circumstances and not an intent to abandon, the statutory clock for
removal for non-use did not apply. The Indian company was a bad-faith
infringer trying to exploit trade barriers.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Intent in Abandonment: Mere non-use of a trademark, even for decades,
does not constitute legal abandonment if the proprietor continuously
renews the registration and shows an intent to retain the rights.

Special Circumstances Excuse: Government import bans, restrictive trade
policies, or wars constitute valid statutory "special circumstances" that
excuse a foreign proprietor's non-use of a registered trademark in India.

cases.title: Macmillan & Company Ltd. v. K. and J. Cooper
cases.facts:
Macmillan & Co. published a book titled Plutarch's Life of Alexander. The
book contained the original historical text written by Sir Thomas North
in 1579 (which was entirely in the public domain). However, Macmillan
significantly edited the text, selected specific passages suitable for
university students, added detailed introduction notes, a glossary, and
marginal notes. K. and J. Cooper published a competing educational book
that directly copied Macmillan's selected text, including the exact
selection of passages and many of the notes. Macmillan sued for copyright
infringement.
cases.issues:
Can copyright subsist in a derivative work (like an abridgment or a
compilation) where the primary underlying text is in the public domain?

What is the quantum of intellectual labor required to grant copyright to
a new arrangement of old material?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Macmillan & Co.)
Macmillan argued that while North's translation of Plutarch was free for
anyone to use, their specific selection and abridgment of the text,
tailored for educational purposes, required immense scholarly skill,
labor, and judgment. They claimed copyright over the compilation and the
newly authored notes, which the defendants had blatantly pirated to save
themselves the effort.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (K. and J. Cooper)
The defendants argued that nobody can claim a monopoly over a public
domain historical text. They argued that cutting out a few paragraphs to
make a book shorter is a mechanical act of scissors and paste. Because
the vast majority of the words in Macmillan's book belonged to a dead
author, there was no original "authorship" to protect.
cases.judgment:
The Privy Council ruled partially in favor of Macmillan. They held that
the selection/abridgment of the text was NOT copyrightable, but the newly
created notes and glossary WERE protected.
cases.reasoning:
This is the absolute bedrock case for copyright in derivative works in
Indian/British jurisprudence. Lord Atkinson established the core test: to
acquire copyright in a derivative work based on public domain material,
the author must impart to the product some quality or character which the
raw material did not possess, differentiating the new work from the old.
The Court ruled that simply chopping out paragraphs to make a book
shorter (scissors and paste) requires no real literary skill or judgment;
therefore, Macmillan's abridgment of the text was not an original work.
However, writing the new educational notes and glossary required
independent scholarly thought, labor, and skill. Because the defendants
copied those notes, they infringed the copyright in that specific
original portion of the book.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Copyright in Derivative Works: A work compiled from public domain
materials is copyrightable only if its creation involved independent
intellectual skill, labor, and judgment, creating a new and distinct
character.

Rejection of Mechanical Labor: Mere mechanical acts, such as simple
editing or cutting texts to length without structural creativity, do not
meet the threshold of "originality" required for copyright protection.

cases.title: Amritdhara Pharmacy v. Satya Deo Gupta
cases.facts:
Amritdhara Pharmacy had been manufacturing a popular Ayurvedic medicinal
preparation under the name "AMRITDHARA" since 1901. Satya Deo Gupta
introduced a similar Ayurvedic medicine in Uttar Pradesh under the name
"LAKSHMANDHARA" in 1923. Decades later, Gupta applied for the
registration of the trademark "LAKSHMANDHARA." Amritdhara Pharmacy
opposed the registration, claiming that the two names were deceptively
similar and that consumers would be confused into believing the two
medicines originated from the same manufacturer.
cases.issues:
What is the legal standard for determining "deceptive similarity" between
two trademarks?

Should the test for confusion be based on a highly observant expert or an
unwary purchaser of average intelligence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Amritdhara Pharmacy)
The appellant argued that "Amrit" and "Lakshman" might be different
words, but both ended with the identical suffix "DHARA," and both were
Ayurvedic medicines sold in identical bottles. They argued that
uneducated consumers in rural India would easily confuse the two products
based on the overall phonetic similarity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Satya Deo Gupta)
Gupta argued that the marks must be compared as a whole. "Amrit" and
"Lakshman" look and sound completely different and have completely
different meanings in Hindi. Furthermore, he argued that "Dhara" (meaning
flow or current) is a common descriptive word in Ayurvedic medicine that
no single entity can monopolize.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Amritdhara Pharmacy, holding
that the marks were deceptively similar, though they allowed
"LAKSHMANDHARA" limited local registration due to honest concurrent use.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court established the absolute bedrock test for trademark
infringement in India: The Unwary Purchaser Test. The Court held that
marks must not be compared side-by-side by a meticulous lawyer with a
magnifying glass. Instead, the court must put itself in the shoes of an
unwary purchaser of average intelligence and imperfect recollection. A
rural consumer buying Ayurvedic medicine will likely remember the overall
structure and the suffix "DHARA." The overall phonetic similarity and the
identical nature of the goods would likely cause cognitive confusion. The
Court ruled that dissecting the mark into "Amrit" and "Dhara" defeats the
purpose of trademark law, which relies on the overall, instantaneous
impression left on the consumer's mind.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Unwary Purchaser Test: Deceptive similarity must be judged from the
perspective of an average consumer with imperfect memory, not an expert
conducting a side-by-side comparison.

Anti-Dissection Rule: Trademarks must be compared as a whole; breaking
them down into component syllables to prove dissimilarity is not legally
permissible.

cases.title: Corn Products Refining Co. v. Shangrila Food Products Ltd.
cases.facts:
Corn Products Refining Co. (an American company) held a registered
trademark in India for "GLUCOVITA," under which they sold glucose powder
mixed with vitamins. Shangrila Food Products later applied to register
the trademark "GLUVITA" for biscuits. Corn Products opposed the
registration. They argued that "GLUCOVITA" and "GLUVITA" were
phonetically identical, and that because glucose is a common ingredient
in biscuits, consumers would assume the biscuits were manufactured by the
famous glucose company.
cases.issues:
Can deceptive similarity exist even when the suffix or prefix of a mark
is slightly altered?

Does an established trademark in one class of goods (glucose) prevent the
registration of a similar mark in a different but allied class
(biscuits)?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Corn Products Refining Co.)
The appellant argued that the phonetic similarity was undeniable.
"Glucovita" and "Gluvita" are almost identical to the ear. They argued
the concept of "trade connection"-since glucose is used in biscuits, the
public would easily assume that the manufacturer of Glucovita had
expanded into making Gluvita biscuits.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Shangrila Food Products)
Shangrila argued that "Gluco" and "Glu" are common abbreviations for
glucose, and "Vita" is a common abbreviation for vitamins. Because both
parts of the word are generic/descriptive, Corn Products cannot claim a
monopoly over them. Furthermore, glucose powder and biscuits are distinct
products sold in different aisles.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Corn Products Refining Co.,
refusing the registration of the "GLUVITA" trademark.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court reinforced the unwary purchaser doctrine and the
concept of a "trade connection." The Court held that absolute identity is
not required for confusion. Phonetically, "Glucovita" and "Gluvita" are
so similar that an average person with an imperfect recollection would be
easily confused. Furthermore, the Court rejected the defense that the
words were just descriptive abbreviations; when combined into a coined
word, it becomes a protectable trademark. Crucially, the Court held that
there was a strong "trade connection" between glucose and biscuits. Since
both are food products and one is an ingredient of the other, an average
consumer would naturally assume a shared commercial origin, leading to
passing off.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Trade Connection Doctrine: Even if goods belong to different statutory
classes, if there is a logical commercial nexus between them (e.g., raw
ingredient and finished food), similar marks will be barred to prevent
consumer confusion regarding the source.

cases.title: Durga Dutt Sharma v. Navaratna Pharmaceutical Laboratories
cases.facts:
