Navaratna Pharmaceutical Laboratories held a registered trademark for the
word "NAVARATNA" for their medicinal preparations. Durga Dutt Sharma ran
an Ayurvedic pharmacy under the name "Navaratna Pharmacy" and sold
medicines using the word "Navaratna" on his packaging. Navaratna
Pharmaceuticals sued Sharma for both trademark infringement and the
common law tort of passing off.
cases.issues:
What is the precise legal distinction between an action for "Trademark
Infringement" and an action for "Passing Off"?

In an infringement suit, is the defendant allowed to argue that the
packaging and get-up of their product are so different that no consumer
would actually be confused?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Respondent (Navaratna Pharmaceutical Labs)
The plaintiff argued that "Navaratna" was their registered trademark. By
using the exact same word on identical medicinal goods, the defendant was
blatantly violating their statutory monopoly, constituting direct
infringement.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Appellant (Durga Dutt Sharma)
Sharma argued that the word "Navaratna" (meaning nine gems) is a common
Ayurvedic term. Moreover, he argued that his packaging, colors, and
bottle shapes were completely different from the plaintiff's. Therefore,
no actual consumer was ever deceived or confused in the marketplace.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Navaratna Pharmaceutical
Laboratories, granting an injunction against the defendant.
cases.reasoning:
This judgment is the bedrock for understanding the duality of trademark
remedies in India. The Supreme Court laid down the absolute distinction
between infringement and passing off.
Passing Off is a common law remedy. In passing off, the defendant can
argue that they added extra material (different packaging, distinct
logos) to clearly distinguish their goods, thereby avoiding actual
consumer confusion.
Infringement, however, is a statutory right. In an infringement action,
the Court held that if the defendant uses a mark that is identical or
deceptively similar to the registered mark, the added matter is entirely
irrelevant. The only test is comparing the two marks themselves. Since
Sharma used the exact registered word "Navaratna," he was guilty of
statutory infringement, and his defense about using different packaging
was legally inadmissible.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Infringement vs. Passing Off: In a statutory infringement suit, the
presence of "added matter" (different packaging, price, or get-up) is
irrelevant as a defense if the core trademark has been copied. Added
matter is only a valid defense in a common law passing off suit.

cases.title: F. Hoffmann-La Roche & Co. Ltd. v. Geoffrey Manner & Co. Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Hoffmann-La Roche (the appellant) manufactured and sold a liquid vitamin
preparation under the registered trademark "DROPOVIT." Geoffrey Manner &
Co. (the respondent) applied for the registration of the trademark
"PROTOVIT" for a similar liquid vitamin preparation. Roche opposed the
registration, arguing that "PROTOVIT" was deceptively similar to
"DROPOVIT" and would cause confusion in pharmacies and among patients.
cases.issues:
Does the sharing of a common suffix ("-VIT") render two pharmaceutical
trademarks deceptively similar?

How should courts weigh the phonetic similarities against the structural
differences of coined words?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Hoffmann-La Roche)
Roche argued that both marks end in "OVIT" and have three syllables. They
argued that in the pharmaceutical sector, where a mistake can be
dangerous, any structural or phonetic resemblance should be interpreted
strictly against the newer applicant to prevent fatal confusion.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Geoffrey Manner & Co.)
The respondent argued that "VIT" is an established, generic abbreviation
for vitamins, which no company can monopolize. The distinctiveness of the
marks lies entirely in their prefixes: "DROP" vs. "PROT." Phonetically,
"Drop" and "Prot" are completely distinct and impossible to confuse.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Geoffrey Manner & Co.,
allowing the registration of "PROTOVIT" and rejecting the claim of
deceptive similarity.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court nuanced the unwary purchaser test by acknowledging the
role of generic suffixes. The Court held that when marks share a common
suffix that is descriptive of the goods (like "VIT" for vitamins), the
court must look closely at the prefix. The Court compared "DROPOVIT" and
"PROTOVIT" and concluded that visually and phonetically, they are
distinct. "Drop" and "Prot" do not sound alike. Furthermore, the Court
noted that both are prescription drugs (Schedule H), meaning they would
be dispensed by trained professionals based on written prescriptions,
further reducing the likelihood of a mix-up between two phonetically
distinct prefixes.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Generic Suffixes: If two marks share a common suffix that is generic or
descriptive of the trade, the test for deceptive similarity relies
heavily on whether the prefixes are sufficiently distinct phonetically
and visually.

cases.title: University of London Press v. University Tutorial Press
cases.facts:
The University of London employed examiners to create mathematics
examination papers for its matriculation exams. A condition of their
employment was that the copyright in these exam papers belonged to the
University. Following the exams, the University Tutorial Press published
a book containing these exact mathematical exam papers, providing their
own answers for students to study. The University of London sued for
copyright infringement, claiming the exam papers were "original literary
works."
cases.issues:
Do standard mathematics examination papers qualify as "original literary
works" capable of copyright protection?

What is the legal standard for "originality" under copyright law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (University of London Press)
The University argued that the examiners expended significant time,
effort, knowledge, and skill to compile, draft, and format the questions.
This intellectual labor transformed standard mathematical concepts into
an original literary compilation.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (University Tutorial Press)
The defendants argued that the mathematical questions were standard,
generic problems drawn from the public domain of mathematics. There was
no literary merit, novel thought, or creative genius involved in writing
them down, and therefore they lacked the "originality" required for
copyright.
cases.judgment:
The Chancery Division ruled in favor of the University of London Press,
holding that the exam papers were original literary works and the
copyright had been infringed.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Peterson delivered the foundational British ruling on copyright
originality. He held that "literary work" is not confined to works of
literature (like novels or poetry); it simply means work expressed in
print or writing. Most importantly, he defined "originality." The Court
held that the word "original" does not mean that the work must be the
expression of original or inventive thought. It merely requires that the
work must not be copied from another work-it must originate from the
author. Because the examiners used their own skill and labor (the "sweat
of the brow") to draft the specific arrangement of questions, the papers
were original to them, regardless of the generic mathematical concepts
involved.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The "Sweat of the Brow" Doctrine: Established the classical threshold for
copyright originality: a work is original if the author expended
independent labor, skill, and effort to create it, without copying it
from elsewhere, regardless of artistic or inventive merit. (Note: This
standard was later rejected by the US in Feist and modified by India in
EBC v. Modak).

cases.title: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co. (1991) (Note: A US Supreme Court case universally taught as the global turning point in Copyright originality jurisprudence).
cases.facts:
Rural Telephone Service Company was a public utility that published a
standard "white pages" telephone directory containing the names, towns,
and telephone numbers of its subscribers, listed alphabetically. Feist
Publications, a publishing company specializing in wider-area
directories, requested a license to use Rural's listings. Rural refused.
Feist proceeded to copy thousands of names and numbers directly from
Rural's directory into their own. Rural sued Feist for copyright
infringement.
cases.issues:
Can factual information (names and phone numbers) be copyrighted?

Does the effort and labor expended in compiling a factual database
("sweat of the brow") grant the compilation copyright protection?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Respondent (Rural Telephone Service Co.)
Rural relied on the historical "sweat of the brow" doctrine. They argued
that they spent significant time, money, and labor driving around to
collect and verify the phone numbers of all local residents. Feist
engaged in blatant piracy by stealing the fruits of their hard labor
without doing the work themselves.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Appellant (Feist Publications)
Feist argued that facts cannot be copyrighted. A name and a phone number
are raw data belonging to the public domain. They argued that compiling
them in standard alphabetical order is entirely obvious and devoid of any
creative authorship.
cases.judgment:
The United States Supreme Court ruled unanimously in favor of Feist
Publications, denying copyright protection to the white pages directory.
cases.reasoning:
Justice O'Connor delivered a landmark judgment that officially killed the
"sweat of the brow" doctrine in US law. The Court held that the sine qua
non (indispensable condition) of copyright is originality. Originality
requires two things: independent creation by the author, and a "modicum
of creativity." Facts themselves are never original. While a compilation
of facts can be copyrighted if the author shows creativity in the
selection or arrangement of the data, Rural's alphabetical listing of all
subscribers was an age-old, standard practice devoid of even the
slightest trace of creativity. Hard work and financial investment alone
do not create a copyright.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Modicum of Creativity Doctrine: Replaced the "sweat of the brow"
doctrine, establishing that mere labor and investment are insufficient
for copyright. A work must possess a minimal degree of creative spark to
be deemed "original."

No Copyright in Facts: Raw data and facts are in the public domain; only
a highly creative arrangement or selection of facts can be protected as a
compilation.

cases.title: Baker v. Selden
cases.facts:
Charles Selden wrote a book titled Selden's Condensed Ledger, or
Bookkeeping Simplified, which explained a novel, simplified system for
accounting. The book included blank forms containing specific columns and
headings designed to put his new accounting system into practice. Selden
obtained a copyright for the book. Years later, Baker published a book
containing accounting forms that achieved the exact same result as
Selden's system, using slightly different columns and headings. Selden's
widow sued Baker for copyright infringement, claiming he stole the
system.
cases.issues:
Does the copyright of a book that describes a useful art, process, or
system also give the author the exclusive right to use and practice that
system?

Can blank forms designed for recording information be copyrighted?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Selden's Widow)
The plaintiff argued that the unique arrangement of columns and headings
was the very essence of Selden's original creation. By creating forms
that utilized the exact same accounting logic, Baker was infringing on
the copyright of the book that birthed the system.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Baker)
Baker argued that copyright only protects the explanation of an idea (the
text of the book), not the idea or system itself. If Selden wanted a
monopoly over a new accounting methodology, he should have filed for a
patent, which requires a much stricter standard of novelty.
cases.judgment:
The US Supreme Court ruled in favor of Baker, dismissing the copyright
infringement claim.
cases.reasoning:
This case established the absolute foundation of the Idea-Expression
Dichotomy. The Court ruled that there is a clear distinction between the
book (which explains a system) and the system itself. Copyright protects
the author's specific words used to explain the accounting method. It
does NOT protect the underlying accounting method. To grant a monopoly
over a useful system via copyright would bypass the rigorous examination
process of patent law.
Furthermore, the Court birthed the Merger Doctrine. It held that where
the use of an idea (the accounting system) dictates a specific expression
(the blank columns and forms necessary to use the system), the idea and
the expression "merge." When they merge, the expression cannot be
copyrighted, because doing so would grant a monopoly over the underlying
idea.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Idea/Expression Dichotomy: Copyright does not protect systems, processes,
or methods of operation, only the literary expression explaining them.

The Merger Doctrine: If an idea can only be expressed in one or a very
limited number of ways, the expression merges with the idea and becomes
uncopyrightable.

cases.title: Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios, Inc. (1984)
cases.facts:
Sony Corporation manufactured and sold the "Betamax" video cassette
recorder (VCR), the first machine allowing consumers to record television
shows at home. Universal City Studios and Walt Disney, owners of massive
television and movie copyrights, sued Sony. They argued that by
manufacturing and selling a machine whose primary purpose was to copy
their copyrighted shows, Sony was liable for "contributory copyright
infringement." They sought an injunction to ban the manufacture of VCRs.
cases.issues:
Can the manufacturer of a technology be held secondarily liable for
copyright infringement committed by the users of that technology?

Is it a "fair use" for a consumer to record a free-to-air television show
for the purpose of watching it at a later time?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Universal City Studios)
Universal argued that Sony knew perfectly well that consumers would use
the Betamax to illegally copy copyrighted movies. By providing the tools
for piracy and profiting from the sale of the machines, Sony was a
contributory infringer aiding massive copyright theft.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Sony Corp.)
Sony argued that the VCR was simply a neutral tool. They demonstrated
that the vast majority of users used the VCR for "time-shifting"-
recording a show they missed to watch it once later. They argued time-
shifting was a fair use, meaning the consumers weren't infringing, and
thus Sony couldn't be a contributory infringer.
cases.judgment:
The US Supreme Court (in a 5-4 decision) ruled in favor of Sony, holding
that the sale of VCRs did not constitute contributory infringement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a monumental judgment that saved the consumer
electronics industry. The Court imported patent law principles into
copyright, establishing the "Staple Article of Commerce" doctrine. The
Court held that a manufacturer cannot be held liable for contributory
infringement if the technology is "capable of substantial non-infringing
uses." The Court then analyzed "time-shifting." Since users were
recording free broadcasts for private, non-commercial home viewing, and
there was no evidence that this harmed the studios' market (in fact, it
expanded viewership), time-shifting was declared a valid "Fair Use."
Because the VCR was widely used for this legitimate, non-infringing
purpose, Sony was completely cleared of liability.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Sony Doctrine (Substantial Non-Infringing Use): The manufacturer of a
product is shielded from secondary copyright liability if the product is
widely capable of commercially significant, non-infringing uses.

Time-Shifting as Fair Use: Recording broadcast television for private,
non-commercial, delayed viewing is a protected fair use.

cases.title: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.
cases.facts:
Roy Orbison wrote the legendary rock ballad "Oh, Pretty Woman." Acuff-
Rose Music held the copyright. The rap group 2 Live Crew requested a
license to create a parody of the song. Acuff-Rose refused. 2 Live Crew
recorded and released the parody anyway, lifting the iconic baseline and
the opening lyrics, but changing the rest of the lyrics to comedic,
vulgar, and degrading rhymes to mock the original's romantic naivety.
Acuff-Rose sued 2 Live Crew for copyright infringement. The lower court
ruled that because the rap song was a "commercial" product sold for
profit, it was presumptively unfair.
cases.issues:
Does the commercial nature of a derivative work automatically disqualify
it from the "fair use" defense?

How much of the original work can a parody legally copy before it becomes
infringement?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Acuff-Rose Music)
The publisher argued that 2 Live Crew stole the "heart" of the song (the
famous baseline) strictly to make money. They argued a commercial parody
is just theft disguised as comedy, and it harms the potential market for
licensing authorized derivative versions of the song.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Campbell / 2 Live Crew)
2 Live Crew argued that parody is a vital form of social commentary and
free speech. A parody, by definition, must copy enough of the original
target so the audience recognizes what is being mocked. They argued that
their rap version was a transformative critique, not a market substitute
for the romantic original.
cases.judgment:
The US Supreme Court ruled in favor of 2 Live Crew, establishing that
commercial parodies can qualify as fair use.
cases.reasoning:
Justice Souter delivered a unanimous, foundational ruling on Fair Use.
The Court rejected the rule that commercial use is presumptively unfair.
Instead, the central inquiry is whether the new work is "transformative."
Does the new work merely supersede the original, or does it add something
new, with a further purpose or different character, altering the first
with new expression, meaning, or message? The Court ruled that 2 Live
Crew's rap song was highly transformative; it took a naive romantic song
and turned it into a cynical, street-smart critique. Regarding the amount
copied, the Court held that a parodist is legally allowed to take the
"heart" of the original work, because a parody must conjure up the
original in the audience's mind to successfully mock it. Finally, a rap
parody does not act as a market substitute for a 1960s rock ballad.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Transformative Use Doctrine: The key test in fair use is whether the
secondary work transforms the original by adding new meaning, expression,
or critique.

Commercial Parody Validation: A parody can successfully claim a fair use
defense even if it is created for pure commercial profit, provided it is
transformative and does not act as a direct market substitute for the
original.

cases.title: Roche Products, Inc. v. Bolar Pharmaceutical Co. (1984) (Note: This US Federal Circuit case birthed the "Bolar Exemption," directly adopted into Indian law as Section 107A of the Patents Act, making it mandatory reading in Indian NLUs).
cases.facts:
Roche Products held a patent for the active ingredient in Dalmane, a
highly successful sleeping pill. The patent was due to expire in early
1984. Bolar Pharmaceutical Co., a generic drug manufacturer, wanted to
launch a generic version the very day the patent expired. To do this,
Bolar imported the patented chemical months before the patent expired and
used it to conduct mandatory bioequivalency testing required by the Food
and Drug Administration (FDA). Roche sued Bolar for patent infringement,
arguing that unauthorized use of a patented chemical during the patent
term is illegal, even for testing.
cases.issues:
Does the use of a patented chemical solely to conduct tests for
regulatory approval constitute patent infringement?

Does the traditional "experimental use" defense cover testing done
strictly for future commercial exploitation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Roche Products)
Roche argued that a patent grants an absolute monopoly. Bolar was using
the patented invention during the patent term to prepare for a massive
commercial launch. This was not a university science experiment; it was a
blatant commercial use aimed at stealing Roche's market share the moment
the patent dropped.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Bolar Pharmaceutical)
Bolar argued the "Experimental Use" exception, claiming they were merely
conducting scientific tests to satisfy FDA bureaucrats. Furthermore, they
argued a massive public policy point: if generic companies must wait for
the patent to expire before they can even begin FDA testing, the patentee
effectively gets a de facto 2-to-3-year extension of their monopoly while
the generic sits in regulatory purgatory, harming public access to cheap
drugs.
cases.judgment:
The Federal Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in favor of Roche, holding
Bolar liable for patent infringement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strict, orthodox reading of patent law. The Court
held that the common law "experimental use" exception is extremely
narrow-it only applies to use for amusement, to satisfy idle curiosity,
or for strictly philosophical inquiry. Bolar's testing was undeniably
conducted for a commercial purpose: to get a product to market.
Therefore, the testing was an infringement. The Court acknowledged
Bolar's valid public policy argument (the de facto extension of the
monopoly), but stated that the courts cannot rewrite patent laws; that is
a job for the legislature.
(Legislative Aftermath: Recognizing the crisis, the US Congress
immediately passed the Hatch-Waxman Act overturning this ruling. This
"Bolar Exemption" allows generics to test during the patent term. India
imported this exact principle into Section 107A of the Patents Act,
forming the backbone of India's massive generic drug export industry).
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Bolar Exemption Origin: This case demonstrated the strict limits of
the common law experimental use defense, prompting global legislative
amendments (like India's Section 107A) that now legally permit generic
manufacturers to use a patented invention during its term solely for
obtaining regulatory approvals.

cases.title: Bishwanath Prasad Radhey Shyam v. Hindustan Metal Industries
cases.facts:
Hindustan Metal Industries held a patent for a specific method and means
of manufacturing utensils. The patented process involved the usual,
traditional steps of scraping and polishing utensils, but utilized a
specific alignment of known machines to increase the speed of production.
Bishwanath Prasad, a competitor, began using a similar method. Hindustan
Metal sued for patent infringement. In response, Bishwanath Prasad filed
a counter-claim seeking the revocation of the patent, arguing that the
so-called "invention" was merely a routine arrangement of existing
machinery and completely lacked any genuine inventive step.
cases.issues:
What is the precise legal threshold for "novelty" and "inventive step"
(non-obviousness) in Indian patent law?

Can a minor, efficiency-boosting alteration to a known industrial process
be considered a patentable invention?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Respondent (Hindustan Metal Industries)
The plaintiff argued that their specific arrangement of the lathe and
polishing tools resulted in a faster, cheaper, and safer manufacturing
process. They argued that because this exact arrangement had never been
published or used before, it was novel, and the increased industrial
efficiency proved it had utility and an inventive step.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Appellant (Bishwanath Prasad Radhey Shyam)
The defendant argued that the patent was a sham. The machines were
standard, the process of polishing was ancient, and putting two known
machines together to work in a sequence is something any ordinary
mechanic in the utensil trade would figure out. They argued this was a
mere "workshop improvement," not an invention.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Bishwanath Prasad, revoking
the patent held by Hindustan Metal Industries.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court delivered the foundational Indian ruling on the
doctrine of obviousness. The Court established that to be patentable, an
improvement must be more than a mere workshop alteration. The test is:
Would a person with ordinary skill in the art, faced with the problem,
find the solution obvious based on existing knowledge? The Court noted
that the plaintiff simply took old, known machines (a lathe and a
scraper) and used them in their expected ways. There was no new technical
synergy or unexpected result. Granting a 20-year monopoly over a routine
mechanical adjustment would stifle ordinary industrial progress.
Therefore, the patent was invalid for lacking an inventive step.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Obviousness Test / Person Having Ordinary Skill In The Art (PHOSITA):
An invention must involve a technical advance that is not obvious to an
ordinary professional in that specific industry. Mere "workshop
improvements" or the collocation of known integers do not cross the
threshold of patentability.

cases.title: Bata India Limited v. Pyare Lal & Co.
cases.facts:
Bata India Limited was (and remains) an iconic, household name in India,
renowned universally for manufacturing and selling footwear. The
defendants, Pyare Lal & Co., based in Meerut, began manufacturing and
selling mattresses, cushions, and polyurethane foam under the brand name
"BATAFOAM." Bata India sued for trademark infringement and the common law
tort of passing off, seeking an injunction to stop the defendants from
using the word "Bata."
cases.issues:
Can the proprietor of a famous trademark prevent others from using the
mark on goods that are entirely dissimilar and unrelated to their own
products?

Does the use of a famous shoe brand name on mattresses cause actionable
consumer confusion?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Bata India Limited)
Bata argued that their trademark had acquired such immense trans-border
and domestic reputation that the word "Bata" was instantly synonymous
with their corporate entity. They argued that any consumer seeing
"Batafoam" on a mattress would automatically, and falsely, assume that
the Bata corporation had diversified its business into home furnishings,
thereby exploiting Bata's goodwill and diluting the brand.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Pyare Lal & Co.)
The defendants argued the strict "classification of goods" defense. They
manufactured mattresses, while the plaintiff manufactured shoes. These
goods are sold in completely different shops to address completely
different needs. They argued that because there was absolutely zero
overlap in the trade channels, no consumer would ever be confused into
buying a mattress thinking it was a shoe.
cases.judgment:
The Allahabad High Court ruled in favor of Bata India Limited, granting
an injunction against the use of the name "Batafoam."
cases.reasoning:
The Court expanded the scope of trademark protection for exceptionally
famous marks, bypassing the traditional "same class of goods"
requirement. The Court held that the name "Bata" was deeply embedded in
the Indian consumer's consciousness. The test for passing off is not
whether the consumer will confuse the products, but whether they will be
confused about the source or sponsorship of the products. Given the
modern trend of massive corporations diversifying into various consumer
goods (e.g., Tata, Reliance), it was entirely reasonable for an ordinary
shopper to see "Batafoam" and assume Bata had started making mattresses.
Allowing this would permit the defendant to illegally free-ride on Bata's
decades of advertising and quality assurance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Protection of Well-Known Marks Across Classes: Extremely famous
trademarks enjoy broad protection against passing off and dilution, even
when the infringing mark is used on entirely dissimilar and unrelated
goods, due to the likelihood of confusion regarding corporate
sponsorship.

cases.title: Krishika Lulla v. Shyam Vithalrao Devkatta
cases.facts:
Shyam Vithalrao Devkatta wrote a story and registered its title, Desi
Boys, with the Film Writers Association in 2008. He shared the synopsis
via email with several people in the film industry but did not produce
the film. In 2011, a Bollywood movie was released titled Desi Boyz,
directed by Rohit Dhawan and produced by Krishika Lulla. The storyline of
the movie was completely different from Devkatta's registered synopsis.
However, Devkatta filed a criminal complaint for copyright infringement
against the producers, claiming they stole his copyrighted title. The
producers petitioned the Supreme Court to quash the criminal proceedings.
cases.issues:
Can a title of a book, movie, or literary work be protected under the
Copyright Act as an "original literary work"?

What are the legal remedies available for the unauthorized use of a movie
title?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Krishika Lulla / Producers)
The producers argued that copyright law protects the substantive
expression of an idea (the script, the dialogue, the narrative), not the
mere title. A title consisting of two common slang words ("Desi" and
"Boys") does not require the skill, labor, and judgment necessary to
qualify as a literary work. They argued that copyrighting short titles
would cripple the creative industry.

B. Arguments for the Respondent (Shyam Vithalrao Devkatta)
Devkatta argued that he coined the phrase specifically for his film
concept and took the formal step of registering it with the writers'
guild. He claimed the title was the central identifier of his
intellectual property, and its unauthorized appropriation caused him
severe financial and professional harm.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of the producers (Krishika
Lulla), quashing the criminal complaint and ruling that titles cannot be
copyrighted.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court settled a long-standing debate in Indian IP law. The
Court unequivocally held that the title of a work does not qualify as a
"literary work" under Section 13 of the Copyright Act. A title is merely
a name used to identify the work; it is too short and lacks the requisite
threshold of original literary expression (the De Minimis doctrine). The
Court clarified that if a title has acquired immense secondary meaning
and goodwill (e.g., Sholay), the owner's only legal remedy against
someone copying it is to file a civil suit for Passing Off under
trademark law, not a suit for copyright infringement. Since Devkatta's
story was never published or made into a film, the title had zero
goodwill, meaning he couldn't even claim passing off.
cases.legalPrinciples:
No Copyright in Titles: The title of a movie, book, or song is generally
not copyrightable as it falls below the threshold of original literary
expression.

Passing Off as the Sole Remedy: The unauthorized use of a famous title is
actionable only under the trademark doctrine of passing off, requiring
the plaintiff to prove established goodwill and secondary meaning.

cases.title: Shree Nath Heritage Liquor Pvt. Ltd. v. Allied Blender & Distillers Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Allied Blender & Distillers (ABD) manufactured and sold a highly popular
brand of whisky named "Officer's Choice." Shree Nath Heritage Liquor
subsequently launched their own brand of whisky named "Collector's
Choice." ABD sued Shree Nath Heritage for trademark infringement and
passing off, arguing that the marks were deceptively similar. Since the
words "Officer" and "Collector" do not look alike and do not sound alike,
the plaintiff based their entire case on the concept of "semantic
similarity."
cases.issues:
Can two trademarks be considered deceptively similar if they are
phonetically and visually distinct but convey the exact same idea or
concept?

Does the "Unwary Purchaser Test" account for cognitive translation and
conceptual association?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Allied Blender & Distillers)
ABD argued that "Officer" and "Collector" are both titles of authority
and power. In the mind of the average Indian consumer, particularly in
the liquor market, a "Collector" (District Collector) is a specific type
of "Officer." Because both marks end with the identical word "Choice,"
consumers would psychologically associate the two brands, believing
"Collector's Choice" is just a variant, premium, or rebranded version of
"Officer's Choice."

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Shree Nath Heritage Liquor)
The defendants argued that trademark infringement requires phonetic or
visual similarity. "Officer" and "Collector" share neither. They argued
that granting a monopoly over a broad concept (persons of authority)
would unfairly restrict the English language and stifle competition.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled in favor of Allied Blender &
Distillers, granting an injunction against the use of the mark
"Collector's Choice."
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fascinating analysis of the psychology of trademark
confusion. The Court upheld the doctrine of Semantic or Conceptual
Similarity. The Court noted that consumers rarely memorize the exact
spelling of a brand; they remember the idea or concept behind the brand.
In the context of Indian society, a "Collector" is the ultimate
"Officer." When an unwary purchaser of average intelligence goes to a
liquor store and recalls the concept of "a person in authority's choice,"
they could easily accept "Collector's Choice" thinking it is the product
they wanted or a sister brand. The conceptual identity, combined with the
identical suffix ("Choice") and identical product category (whisky),
created a strong likelihood of deceptive confusion.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Semantic / Conceptual Confusion: Trademark infringement can occur even
without visual or phonetic similarity if the rival mark utilizes words
that convey the exact same idea, concept, or meaning as the registered
mark, particularly when the target consumer demographic relies on
conceptual recall.

cases.title: ICC Development (International) Ltd. v. Arvee Enterprises
cases.facts:
ICC Development (International) Ltd. (IDI) was the commercial arm of the
International Cricket Council and owned all commercial rights to the 2003
Cricket World Cup. IDI had official sponsors who paid millions for
exclusive association rights. Arvee Enterprises and Philips India
launched promotional campaigns offering consumers who bought Philips
products the chance to win "Ticket[s] to the World Cup." Philips was not
an official sponsor. IDI sued Philips for "ambush marketing" and passing
off, arguing that Philips was illegally free-riding on the goodwill of
the World Cup and depriving official sponsors of their exclusive rights.
cases.issues:
Is "ambush marketing" a legally recognized statutory or common law
offense in India?

Can the organizers of an event claim an absolute intellectual property
monopoly over the event's generic name (e.g., "World Cup")?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (ICC / IDI)
IDI argued that organizing the World Cup requires massive investment.
Official sponsors pay a premium for exclusive rights to associate their
brand with the event. By running a contest giving away World Cup tickets,
Philips was ambushing the event-gaining the commercial benefits of
association without paying the sponsorship fees, thereby committing the
tort of passing off and unfair competition.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Philips India)
Philips argued that they were not using the official ICC logos, mascots,
or registered trademarks. They simply purchased legal, valid tickets to
the event and gave them away as prizes. They argued that "World Cup" is a
generic dictionary term describing a global tournament, not a trademark.
Restricting a company from using generic words in factual marketing
violates the freedom of commercial speech.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Philips India, dismissing the
ICC's application for an injunction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court firmly checked the overreach of sports IP monopolies. The Court
held that "Ambush Marketing" is not an actionable offense under Indian
trademark or copyright law unless the defendant actually uses the
plaintiff's specific registered trademarks, logos, or falsely claims to
be an "official sponsor." Merely running a contest offering legally
purchased tickets is an ordinary business practice. Furthermore, the
Court rejected the idea that an event organizer can monopolize generic
words like "World Cup." The Court also rejected the claim of "personality
rights" for the event, noting that the right of publicity belongs
strictly to living human beings, not to corporate events.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Legality of Ambush Marketing: Unless specific trademarks are infringed or
a false claim of official sponsorship is made, "ambush marketing" (free-
riding on the public hype of an event) is a legitimate competitive
business practice, not an IP infringement.

No Monopolies on Event Names: Event organizers cannot claim passing off
or trademark infringement over the generic use of terms like "World Cup"
in factual commercial campaigns.

cases.title: Dabur India Ltd. v. Colgate Palmolive India Ltd.
cases.facts:
Dabur India commanded a dominant 80% market share in the Ayurvedic red
tooth powder market with its flagship product, "Dabur Lal Dant Manjan."
Colgate Palmolive, aiming to promote its white toothpaste, aired a
television commercial featuring a Bollywood actor. The ad showed a
consumer using a generic, unnamed "red tooth powder." The actor then
demonstrated the abrasive nature of the red powder by rubbing it on a
pair of glasses, leaving scratches, and likened using red tooth powder to
brushing teeth with sandpaper. Dabur sued Colgate for trade disparagement
and sought an injunction.
cases.issues:
Does disparaging a generic class of products (red tooth powder)
constitute actionable trade disparagement against a specific company
whose brand is not explicitly named?

Is pointing out the generic flaws of a product category protected as
commercial free speech?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Dabur India)
Dabur argued that because they held an 80% market share, an attack on
"red tooth powder" was an undeniable, targeted attack on Dabur Lal Dant
Manjan. They argued the commercial was maliciously false and designed to
terrify rural consumers into believing that Dabur's product was actively
destroying their teeth, causing massive and immediate financial damage to
Dabur's goodwill.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Colgate Palmolive)
Colgate argued the defense of generic disparagement. They claimed they
never named Dabur, nor did they show Dabur's specific packaging. They
were merely educating consumers that all traditional tooth powders are
highly abrasive compared to modern toothpaste. They argued that truthful
consumer education is protected commercial speech and not actionable
disparagement.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Dabur India, granting an
injunction to stop the broadcast of the commercial.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reinforced the doctrine of Generic Disparagement. The Court
held that a plaintiff does not need to be explicitly named in an
advertisement to claim disparagement. If the plaintiff holds a dominant
market share in a specific category, denigrating that entire category
causes direct, quantifiable harm to the plaintiff. The Court drew a
strict line regarding comparative advertising: a company is free to say
"my toothpaste is better than your powder," but it cannot cross the line
to say "your powder is like sandpaper and will destroy your teeth."
Highlighting a competitor's alleged flaws in a manner designed to incite
fear and disgust constitutes illegal trade defamation, overriding the
defense of generic free speech.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Generic Disparagement is Actionable: Denigrating an entire class of goods
constitutes trade disparagement against the market leader of that class,
even if their specific trademark or trade dress is not displayed.

Limits of Commercial Free Speech: Advertisements cannot be used to
maliciously defame or falsely portray a competitor's product category as
dangerous or harmful.

cases.title: Godfrey Phillips India Ltd. v. Girnar Food & Beverages Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Godfrey Phillips India sold a premium brand of tea under the trademark
"Super Cup." They had invested heavily in advertising and claimed the
mark was highly recognized. Girnar Food & Beverages subsequently launched
their own brand of tea and named it "Super Cup." Godfrey Phillips filed a
suit for trademark infringement and passing off in the High Court,
seeking an injunction. The High Court refused the injunction, stating
that the words were purely descriptive. Godfrey Phillips appealed to the
Supreme Court.
cases.issues:
Can a trademark composed entirely of common, laudatory, and descriptive
words (like "Super" and "Cup") be granted a statutory monopoly?

Under what circumstances can a descriptive trademark be protected through
a common law passing off action?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Godfrey Phillips India)
The appellant acknowledged that "Super" and "Cup" are common words.
However, they argued that through years of exclusive use and massive
advertising expenditure, the specific combination "Super Cup" had lost
its primary descriptive meaning and acquired a secondary meaning in the
tea market, pointing exclusively to their brand.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Girnar Food & Beverages)
The respondents argued that "Super" is a standard laudatory term (meaning
very good), and "Cup" describes the vessel used to drink tea. Combining
two generic dictionary words does not create a distinctive trademark.
Granting a monopoly over "Super Cup" would prevent other tea merchants
from legally describing their own tea as a super cup of tea.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Godfrey Phillips, holding
that a passing off action is maintainable for descriptive marks if
secondary meaning is proven, and remanded the case back for a full trial.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court clarified the law regarding descriptive trademarks. The
Court agreed that, as a general rule, purely descriptive or laudatory
words cannot be registered as trademarks because they belong to the
public domain. However, the Court highlighted the crucial exception:
Acquired Distinctiveness (Secondary Meaning). Even the most generic
descriptive words can be protected under the common law of passing off if
the plaintiff can prove, with empirical evidence (sales data, advertising
spend, consumer surveys), that the public no longer sees the words as a
description of the product, but specifically as a badge of origin for the
plaintiff's brand. Since it is a matter of factual evidence, it cannot be
dismissed summarily, allowing Godfrey Phillips to proceed to trial to
prove their acquired distinctiveness.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Protection of Descriptive Marks: Laudatory and descriptive words are
prima facie unprotectable, but they can function as valid trademarks and
sustain a passing off action if the proprietor proves they have acquired
absolute secondary meaning in the marketplace.

cases.title: Sajeev Pillai v. Venu Kunnappilli
cases.facts:
Sajeev Pillai, an acclaimed scriptwriter, wrote a detailed historical
script for a massive Malayalam epic film titled Mamangam. He was also
initially hired to direct the film. After completing a few schedules, the
producer (Venu Kunnappilli) fired Pillai as the director and replaced
him. The new director and producer then significantly altered, mutilated,
and rewrote Pillai's original script to make it more commercially viable,
without Pillai's consent. Pillai filed a suit under Section 57 of the
Copyright Act, seeking an injunction to stop the release of the film,
claiming a violation of his moral rights as an author.
cases.issues:
Does a scriptwriter retain "moral rights" (paternity and integrity) over
their script even after transferring the economic copyright to the film's
producer?

Does the producer's right to adapt a script for a film override the
author's right to prevent the mutilation of their work?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Sajeev Pillai)
Pillai argued that Section 57 (Author's Special Rights) is absolute and
unassignable. Even if the producer owned the copyright to make the film,
they did not own the right to butcher his artistic vision. The extensive,
unauthorized alterations distorted the historical accuracy and artistic
merit of his script, prejudicing his honor and reputation as a writer.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Venu Kunnappilli / Producer)
The producer relied on the standard industry practice. They argued that
once a script is sold for a movie, the producer invests millions and has
the absolute economic right to tweak the script to suit audience tastes,
budgets, and actor capabilities. They argued that stopping the release of
a massive film over subjective "moral rights" would cause catastrophic
financial ruin to innocent investors.
cases.judgment:
The Kerala High Court ruled in favor of Sajeev Pillai, granting an
injunction protecting his moral rights and demanding that the producer
either restore the original script or credit Pillai properly while
removing the distortions.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a powerful defense of creators' rights against
corporate producers. The Court ruled that under Section 57 of the
Copyright Act, an author's moral rights are supreme and exist entirely
independently of the economic copyright. Selling a script gives the
producer the right to make the movie, but it does NOT give them a license
to distort, mutilate, or modify the core literary work in a way that
damages the author's reputation. The Court held that a film producer
cannot use their financial investment as an excuse to trample the
statutory dignity of the writer. The mutilation of the historical script
was deemed prejudicial to Pillai's honor, validating his claim.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Supremacy of Moral Rights in Cinema: A scriptwriter's moral right to
integrity (Section 57) cannot be extinguished by contract. Producers who
substantially alter or mutilate a purchased script without consent are
liable to be injuncted, even if they own the economic copyright to the
film.

cases.title: Kent RO Systems Ltd. v. Amit Kotak
cases.facts:
Kent RO Systems, a leading manufacturer of water purifiers in India, held
registered patents and industrial designs for their specific water
purifiers. They discovered that several third-party sellers were listing
counterfeit Kent products and purifiers that infringed on their designs
on eBay India. Kent filed a suit against both the sellers and eBay.
Crucially, Kent sought an injunction forcing eBay to proactively screen
and filter all future listings on its website to ensure no infringing
products were ever uploaded, rather than Kent having to report them
individually.
cases.issues:
Under the Information Technology (IT) Act, does an e-commerce
intermediary have a legal obligation to proactively screen user uploads
for potential IP infringement?

Does the "safe harbor" protection for intermediaries depend on proactive
policing or reactive takedowns?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Kent RO Systems)
Kent argued that eBay profits from every sale made on its platform,
including counterfeit sales. They argued it is unfair and practically
impossible for a patent holder to manually search millions of daily
listings. Since eBay possesses the technological algorithms to filter
content, they have an equitable duty to proactively prevent IP
infringement before the listings go live.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (eBay India)
eBay relied strictly on Section 79 of the IT Act. They argued they are a
passive marketplace connecting buyers and sellers. Imposing a duty to
proactively screen listings for patent/design infringement would require
eBay to act as an unauthorized judicial authority, deciding complex IP
disputes on the fly. This would cripple the e-commerce industry.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of eBay, refusing to grant the
injunction that would force the platform to proactively screen for IP
infringement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reinforced the vital "Notice and Takedown" regime established
under Indian law (aligning with the MySpace ruling). The Court held that
Section 79 of the IT Act clearly exempts intermediaries from liability
provided they take down infringing content upon receiving actual
knowledge (a specific notice from the rights holder). The law imposes no
statutory obligation on an e-commerce platform to proactively police its
own website for intellectual property violations. To force eBay to screen
every listing would transform them into a global IP tribunal, destroying
the safe harbor provision. The burden of vigilance lies on the IP owner
to locate the infringement and issue the takedown notice; it cannot be
outsourced to the intermediary.
cases.legalPrinciples:
No Proactive Policing for Intermediaries: E-commerce platforms and
intermediaries are legally shielded from proactive filtering obligations.
Their duty to remove infringing IP is strictly reactive, triggered only
upon receiving specific, targeted notices from the rights holders.

cases.title: Cello Household Products v. Modware India
cases.facts:
Cello, a prominent household plastics manufacturer, designed and launched
a unique water bottle named the "PURO." The bottle featured a highly
distinctive two-tone color scheme, an oval-shaped dimpled surface, a
specific flip-top cap, and an ergonomic grip. Cello did not register it
as a design. Modware India subsequently launched a water bottle named
"Kuro," which was an exact, identical replica of Cello's Puro bottle in
shape, color combinations, and text placement. Since they lacked a design
registration, Cello sued Modware for the common law tort of passing off
their trade dress.
cases.issues:
Can the purely functional shape of an everyday household item (a water
bottle) be protected as a trademark/trade dress under the tort of passing
off?

How does a plaintiff establish that the physical shape of an unregistered
product has acquired secondary meaning?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Cello Household Products)
Cello argued that while a water bottle is a functional item, the specific
aesthetic choices they made (the two-tone colors, the dimples, the wavy
grip) were entirely arbitrary and non-functional. Through massive sales
and advertising, this specific visual "get-up" (trade dress) had acquired
immense secondary meaning. Modware's exact replica was a bad-faith
attempt to deceive consumers.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Modware India)
Modware argued that a water bottle is a utilitarian good. The shape of a
bottle is dictated by its function (holding water). Under trademark law,
functional shapes cannot be monopolized. Since Cello failed to register
the bottle under the Designs Act, they left the aesthetic shape in the
public domain for competitors to freely copy.
cases.judgment:
The Bombay High Court ruled in favor of Cello, granting an injunction
against Modware for passing off the trade dress.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a blow against blatant industrial copying. The Court
acknowledged that while you cannot trademark the functional requirement
of a bottle (it must hold liquid and have a cap), you can protect the
specific, capricious, and aesthetic non-functional features of the
bottle's design (Trade Dress). The Court noted that there are thousands
of ways to design a water bottle. The fact that Modware chose to copy
Cello's exact dimples, exact colors, and exact font proved that Modware
wasn't copying the "function"; they were deliberately copying Cello's
"goodwill." Cello proved acquired distinctiveness through high sales
volumes, establishing that the public associated that specific shape
solely with Cello.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Trade Dress in Functional Items: The aesthetic, non-functional visual
features (shape, color, get-up) of an everyday utilitarian product can
function as a protectable trademark if they acquire secondary meaning.

Intent to Deceive: When a competitor perfectly replicates a highly unique
but unregistered product design, courts will presume a bad-faith intent
to pass off, granting equitable relief to the original creator.

cases.title: CTR Manufacturing Industries Ltd. v. Sergi Transformer Explosion Prevention Technologies
cases.facts:
CTR Manufacturing held a patent for a system and method preventing
explosions and fires in electrical transformers. Sergi, a competing
company, began manufacturing a highly similar explosion prevention
system. CTR filed a suit for patent infringement seeking an interim
injunction. Sergi counter-claimed that CTR's patent was invalid for
obviousness and prior publication, pointing to an earlier patent granted
to a French entity that allegedly disclosed the same fundamental
mechanism for draining oil and injecting nitrogen to prevent transformer
fires.
cases.issues:
What is the standard for determining "prior publication" to invalidate a
patent at the interim injunction stage?

How should courts evaluate the "inventive step" when an invention
involves a new arrangement of known elements?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (CTR Manufacturing)
CTR argued that while individual elements of their system (valves,
nitrogen injection) were known, the specific, sequential integration of
these elements to create a rapid-response explosion prevention system was
novel and non-obvious. They argued their patent enjoyed a presumption of
validity and Sergi's product was a mechanical equivalent.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Sergi Transformer)
Sergi argued that the French patent already disclosed the concept of
preventing explosions by rapidly draining oil and injecting inert gas.
They argued CTR's patent was merely a workshop improvement-a routine
engineering adjustment of existing prior art that lacked any genuine
inventive spark.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ultimately ruled in favor of CTR
Manufacturing, staying the order of the High Court that had revoked the
patent, and directed a fresh, expedited trial on merits.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court expressed strong disapproval of invalidating complex
technology patents at the summary/interim stage based merely on affidavit
evidence. The Court reiterated that determining "obviousness" and parsing
through prior art documents requires a rigorous technical trial with
expert cross-examination. A patent cannot be summarily struck down simply
because its individual components existed previously; the "inventive
step" often lies in the novel combination and synergistic result of those
components. By protecting CTR's patent pending a full trial, the Court
reinforced the statutory presumption of validity that attaches to granted
patents.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Presumption of Patent Validity: Granted patents carry a presumption of
validity that cannot be easily displaced at the interim stage without
substantive expert evidence testing the claims of prior art and
obviousness.

cases.title: Banyan Tree Holding (UK) Ltd. v. A. Murali Krishna Reddy
cases.facts:
Banyan Tree Holding, a UK-based hospitality company, held the trademark
for the "Banyan Tree" brand of luxury resorts. The defendants, based in
Hyderabad, India, began a real estate project under the name "Banyan Tree
Retreat." Banyan Tree UK filed a trademark infringement and passing off
suit in the Delhi High Court. The defendants challenged the territorial
jurisdiction of the Delhi High Court, arguing they had no physical
presence, office, or property in Delhi. The plaintiff argued that because
the defendant's website was accessible in Delhi, the court had
jurisdiction.
cases.issues:
Does the mere accessibility of a website in a particular jurisdiction
confer territorial jurisdiction upon the courts of that place for a
trademark infringement suit?

What is the legal test to establish jurisdiction over internet-based IP
infringement in India?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Banyan Tree Holding)
The plaintiff argued that the internet erases physical boundaries.
Because a consumer sitting in Delhi could access the defendant's website,
view the infringing trademark, and potentially book a property, a part of
the cause of action arose in Delhi.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (A. Murali Krishna Reddy)
The defendant argued that their website was universally accessible, but
their business was entirely localized in Hyderabad. They had not made a
single sale in Delhi. Allowing jurisdiction purely based on website
accessibility would mean an internet business could be maliciously sued
in any court across the globe.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled in favor of the defendants,
holding that the Delhi High Court lacked territorial jurisdiction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered India's foundational ruling on internet jurisdiction,
adopting the US "Purposeful Availment" (Zippo) test. The Court held that
mere accessibility of a passive website in a specific state does not
grant jurisdiction to that state's courts. To establish jurisdiction, the
plaintiff must prima facie plead and prove that the defendant
"purposefully directed" its activities toward the forum state. The
website must be highly interactive, and the defendant must have
specifically targeted consumers in that jurisdiction, resulting in actual
commercial transactions. Since Banyan Tree UK could not prove that the
Hyderabad builders specifically targeted Delhi residents or concluded
commercial transactions in Delhi, the court had no jurisdiction.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Internet Jurisdiction (Purposeful Availment): In online trademark
disputes, territorial jurisdiction is only established if the defendant's
website is interactive and actively targets or purposefully avails itself
of the commercial market within the court's specific geographic
territory.

cases.title: MRF Limited v. Metro Tyres Ltd.
cases.facts:
MRF Limited produced a highly stylized television commercial for its
"Nylogrip Ezeeride" tires. The commercial featured specific visual
sequences, camera angles, color palettes, and a thematic narrative. Metro
Tyres subsequently released a commercial for their own tires. Metro's
commercial did not literally copy any actual footage from MRF's
commercial (there was no physical duplication/dubbing). However, Metro's
commercial meticulously recreated the overall aesthetic, sequence of
events, and thematic feel of MRF's advertisement. MRF sued for copyright
infringement of their "cinematograph film."
cases.issues:
Does copyright in a cinematograph film only protect against the exact
physical duplication (dubbing/piracy) of the recording?

Can a newly shot film infringe the copyright of an earlier film if it
substantially copies the underlying arrangement, sequence, and aesthetic
expression?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (MRF Limited)
MRF argued that a cinematograph film is an original work of authorship.
Copyright protects the creative choices of the director-the sequence,
pacing, lighting, and narrative arrangement. Metro's ad was a "colorable
imitation" that stole the core creative expression of MRF's film, even
though they used different actors and shot new footage.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Metro Tyres)
Metro Tyres relied on a literal reading of Section 14(d) of the Copyright
Act, which grants the owner the right to "make a copy of the film." They
argued that in Indian law, copyright in a film only prevents physical
piracy (making a duplicate print or DVD). Because they shot their own
film from scratch, they did not "make a copy" of the physical recording,
and thus committed no infringement.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of MRF Limited, granting an
injunction against Metro Tyres for copyright infringement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court expanded the scope of copyright protection for cinematograph
films. The Court rejected the narrow interpretation that film copyright
only prevents physical piracy. Harmonizing Indian law with the Berne
Convention, the Court held that a film is recognized as an original,
composite work of intellectual creation. If a subsequent film
substantially, qualitatively, and quantitatively copies the fundamental
creative expression, arrangement, and sequence of an earlier film, it
constitutes copyright infringement. The Court found that Metro Tyres had
brazenly recreated the specific aesthetic and narrative arc of the MRF
commercial, crossing the line from borrowing an "idea" into stealing
protected "expression."
cases.legalPrinciples:
Substantial Similarity in Films: Copyright infringement in a
cinematograph film is not limited to physical duplication; it extends to
unauthorized, substantial remakes or colorable imitations that replicate
the core creative expression and sequence of the original work.

cases.title: Gautam Gambhir v. D.A.P. & Co.
cases.facts:
Gautam Gambhir, a famous Indian international cricketer, discovered a
chain of restaurants and pubs operating in Delhi under the names "Gautam
Gambhir's Ghungroo" and "Hawalat by Gautam Gambhir." The cricketer filed
a suit for trademark infringement, passing off, and violation of his
personality rights. He claimed the restaurants were unlawfully cashing in
on his celebrity status, misleading the public into believing he endorsed
or owned the pubs. The defendant, however, was an actual businessman
whose legal birth name was also Gautam Gambhir, and he had been running
businesses under his own name.
cases.issues:
Does a celebrity's right of publicity completely extinguish a private
citizen's statutory right to use their own birth name in a commercial
business?

What are the limits of the "bona fide use of own name" defense under
Section 35 of the Trade Marks Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Cricketer Gautam Gambhir)
The plaintiff argued that his name possessed massive, trans-industry
goodwill. When the public sees the name "Gautam Gambhir" on a billboard,
they immediately associate it with the cricketer. He argued the defendant
was using the name maliciously to create a false association and pass off
the restaurants as being owned by the celebrity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Businessman Gautam Gambhir)
The defendant argued Section 35 of the Trade Marks Act, claiming an
absolute right to use his own name. He proved his name was genuinely
Gautam Gambhir. Furthermore, he argued that nowhere in his restaurants
did he use any cricketing imagery, photos of the player, or logos
associated with cricket. He was operating an entirely unrelated
hospitality business.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of the defendant (the businessman),
dismissing the cricketer's application for an injunction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a vital balance between personality rights and statutory
trademark defenses. The Court held that the right to use one's own name
in a bona fide manner is deeply protected by law. A celebrity cannot
claim an absolute global monopoly over a common Indian name. The crucial
test is bona fides (good faith). The Court noted that the defendant did
not use any cricket bats, balls, or images of the cricketer in his pub's
branding. He simply used his own name alongside distinct restaurant
logos. Because there was no active misrepresentation or intent to deceive
the public into assuming a connection with the cricketer, the defendant's
use of his own name was entirely bona fide and protected by Section 35.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Bona Fide Name Defense vs. Personality Rights: A celebrity's right of
publicity cannot prevent an ordinary citizen from using their own
identical birth name in commerce, provided the citizen uses it in good
faith without adopting any imagery or trade dress that actively implies
an association with the celebrity.

cases.title: John Richard Brady v. Chemical Process Equipments P. Ltd.
cases.facts:
John Richard Brady invented a specialized fodder production unit. To
explore manufacturing the unit in India, Brady entered into negotiations
with Chemical Process Equipments. During these negotiations, under strict
conditions of confidentiality, Brady shared his highly detailed technical
drawings, blueprints, and know-how with the Indian company. The
negotiations failed, and no formal contract was signed. Shortly after,
the Indian company began manufacturing and selling a fodder production
unit that was an exact replica of Brady's design. Brady sued for breach
of confidentiality and copyright infringement.
cases.issues:
Can the unauthorized use of technical drawings and know-how be restrained
under the law of trade secrets and confidentiality, even in the absence
of a formal non-disclosure agreement (NDA)?

Does Indian law recognize the "Springboard Doctrine" regarding
confidential information?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (John Richard Brady)
Brady argued that the drawings were his intellectual property, imparted
to the defendants for a very specific, limited purpose (evaluating a
joint venture). By utilizing those private blueprints to manufacture
their own machine, the defendants committed a gross breach of equitable
trust and copyright infringement of the artistic drawings.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Chemical Process Equipments)
The defendants argued that there was no binding, written confidentiality
contract. Furthermore, they argued that once the machine concept was
known, they were free to reverse-engineer or develop their own version,
claiming their machine was independently designed.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of John Richard Brady, granting a
sweeping injunction against the Indian company based on breach of
confidentiality.
cases.reasoning:
This case firmly embedded the Springboard Doctrine into Indian Trade
Secret jurisprudence. The Court held that the law of confidence does not
strictly require a written contract; it arises from equity. When
information is shared in circumstances implying confidence (like a
business pitch), the recipient has an absolute equitable duty not to use
it for unauthorized purposes.
The Court adopted the Springboard Doctrine: a person who receives
confidential information cannot use it as a "springboard" to jump ahead
of competitors. Even if the Indian company could have eventually designed
the machine through independent research or reverse engineering, they
bypassed years of R&D by illegitimately using Brady's blueprints. The
Court will strip the infringer of this unfair head-start through
injunctions.
cases.legalPrinciples:
The Springboard Doctrine: A party who receives confidential information
cannot use it as an unfair shortcut to accelerate their own commercial
development, even in the absence of a formal NDA. Equity protects trade
secrets communicated in trust.

cases.title: Time Incorporated v. Lokesh Srivastava
cases.facts:
Time Incorporated, the publisher of the globally renowned "TIME"
magazine, held registered trademarks in India. Lokesh Srivastava, an
Indian publisher, began printing and selling a magazine titled "TIME ASIA
SANSKARAN." The defendant directly copied the iconic red border, the
specific font, and the exact stylized layout of the TIME magazine cover.
The defendant did not appear in court, leading to an ex-parte proceeding.
Time Inc. sought not only a permanent injunction but also heavily pressed
for "punitive damages."
cases.issues:
Are Indian courts empowered to award "punitive" or "exemplary" damages in
cases of blatant intellectual property infringement?

What is the standard for calculating damages when the infringer
deliberately stays away from the judicial proceedings?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Time Incorporated)
Time Inc. argued that an injunction is no longer a sufficient deterrent.
Counterfeiters factor regular compensatory damages into their cost of
doing business. Furthermore, by refusing to appear in court, the
defendant prevented the plaintiff from calculating actual lost profits.
Time Inc. argued that the court must award massive punitive damages to
actively punish the infringer and send a deterrent message to the market.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Lokesh Srivastava)
(Ex-parte proceeding; the defendant did not mount a defense).
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Time Incorporated, granting a
permanent injunction and, for the first time, awarding significant
punitive damages (₹5 Lakhs) alongside compensatory damages.
cases.reasoning:
The Court revolutionized the landscape of IP damages in India.
Historically, courts only awarded compensatory damages (making the
plaintiff whole). The Court noted that in a developing economy, flagrant
IP piracy was rampant. If courts only issue injunctions, infringers have
nothing to lose by trying. The Court held that the time had come to
introduce Punitive Damages-damages designed specifically to punish the
wrongdoer and deter others. Because the defendant deliberately copied a
globally famous mark in bad faith and then contemptuously ignored the
judicial process, the Court held they must be financially penalized
beyond mere compensation to wipe out the ill-gotten gains of piracy.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Punitive Damages in IP: Indian courts have the equitable jurisdiction to
award punitive (exemplary) damages in cases of flagrant, bad-faith
intellectual property infringement to actively deter counterfeiting.

cases.title: Patel Field Marshal Agencies v. P.M. Diesels Ltd.
cases.facts:
P.M. Diesels filed a civil suit for trademark infringement against Patel
Field Marshal. During the suit, Patel Field Marshal raised a defense that
P.M. Diesels' trademark registration was invalid. After the civil suit
was filed, but without asking for the civil court's permission, Patel
Field Marshal filed a rectification petition before the statutory
authority (the IPAB) to cancel the trademark. The litigation stalled as
the parties argued over which forum had jurisdiction: Does the civil
court have to wait for the IPAB, or is the IPAB petition invalid because
it was filed without the civil court's leave?
cases.issues:
Under Section 111/124 of the Trade Marks Act, if a civil suit for
infringement is pending, can a defendant independently approach the
IPAB/Registrar to cancel the plaintiff's trademark?

Does the civil court serve as a mandatory gatekeeper to assess the "prima
facie tenability" of the invalidity claim before rectification
proceedings can begin?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Appellant (Patel Field Marshal)
The appellant argued that the statutory right to seek cancellation
(rectification) of an invalid trademark is an independent right. They
argued that they do not need the permission of a civil judge to exercise
their statutory right before the specialized IP tribunal, regardless of
whether a civil suit is currently pending.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (P.M. Diesels)
The respondent argued that Section 124 mandates a strict procedure to
prevent parallel proceedings and conflicting judgments. Once a civil suit
is initiated, the civil court is seized of the matter. A defendant cannot
secretly run to the IPAB to derail the suit. They must first convince the
civil judge that their invalidity defense has merit.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of P.M. Diesels, holding that
once a civil suit is filed, the defendant cannot initiate rectification
proceedings without the explicit leave (permission) of the civil court.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court meticulously interpreted Section 124 of the Trade Marks
Act to eliminate parallel litigation. The Court ruled that if no civil
suit is pending, anyone can approach the IPAB for rectification. However,
the moment a civil suit for infringement is instituted, the civil court
gains primacy. If the defendant wants to claim the trademark is invalid,
the civil court must first frame a specific "issue" on validity. Only if
the civil court finds the invalidity claim "prima facie tenable" will it
stay the suit and give the defendant 3 months to file the rectification
petition. If the defendant fails to ask the civil court, or if the civil
court finds the claim frivolous, the defendant legally abandons their
right to seek rectification.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Primacy of the Civil Court (Section 124): In pending trademark
infringement suits, defendants are legally barred from initiating
parallel rectification proceedings before statutory authorities without
first obtaining the explicit leave of the presiding civil court.

cases.title: M/s Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. v. Coca Cola Company
cases.facts:
Coca Cola entered into a franchise agreement with Gujarat Bottling Co.
(GBC) in India. The agreement contained a strict negative covenant:
during the period of the agreement, GBC was prohibited from
manufacturing, selling, or dealing in any beverages competing with Coca
Cola. A corporate dispute arose, and the promoters of GBC transferred
their shares to a group affiliated with Pepsi (Coca Cola's arch-rival).
GBC then gave notice to terminate the agreement and began preparing to
bottle Pepsi. Coca Cola sued for an injunction to enforce the negative
covenant and prevent GBC from dealing with Pepsi.
cases.issues:
Is a negative covenant in a commercial franchise agreement (restricting
the franchisee from dealing with competitors) void as an illegal
"restraint of trade" under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act?

Under what circumstances will courts grant injunctions to enforce
negative covenants in IP and licensing agreements?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Respondent (Coca Cola Company)
Coca Cola argued that the negative covenant was a standard, vital element
of global franchise agreements. They were sharing trade secrets,
proprietary syrup formulations, and massive brand goodwill with GBC.
Allowing GBC to simultaneously bottle a rival product using Coca Cola's
infrastructure and know-how would destroy their IP. They argued the
restriction was reasonable and operative only during the contract.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Appellant (Gujarat Bottling Co.)
GBC relied on Section 27 of the Contract Act, which states that every
agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful
profession, trade, or business is void. They argued the clause was an
illegal monopoly tactic by Coca Cola to crush competition.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India ruled in favor of Coca Cola, upholding the
validity of the negative covenant and granting the injunction against
GBC.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court laid down the definitive rule on negative covenants in
Indian commercial law. The Court drew a strict line between covenants
operative during the term of the contract and those operative after
termination. The Court held that a negative covenant designed to apply
during the subsistence of an active franchise or licensing agreement is
not a restraint of trade under Section 27. It is a legitimate mechanism
to advance trade, ensure the franchisee's undivided loyalty, and protect
the franchisor's intellectual property and trade secrets. Because GBC was
still legally bound by the active agreement, Coca Cola had the absolute
equitable right to an injunction to stop them from utilizing the shared
infrastructure to benefit a direct competitor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Validity of In-Term Negative Covenants: Exclusivity clauses and negative
covenants operative during the lifespan of a franchise, employment, or IP
licensing agreement are legally valid and enforceable, not constituting
an illegal restraint of trade.

cases.title: Koninklijke Philips Electronics NV v. Rajesh Bansal
cases.facts:
Philips, a global electronics giant, held the essential patent for
"Channel Decoding" technology, a mandatory Standard Essential Patent
(SEP) required to manufacture DVD players globally. Rajesh Bansal and his
company imported and assembled DVD players in India without obtaining a
license from Philips. Philips filed a suit for patent infringement. This
case was unique because, unlike most SEP cases that stall at the interim
injunction stage, this case proceeded through a massive, multi-year full
technical trial with expert cross-examinations.
cases.issues:
How does a patentee conclusively prove that their patent is a "Standard
Essential Patent" (SEP) during a full trial?

What is the methodology for calculating actual damages/royalties for SEP
infringement upon the conclusion of a trial?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff (Philips)
Philips presented expert witnesses who mapped the claims of their patent
directly onto the technical specifications of the global DVD standard
published by the standard-setting organization. They argued that since
the defendant's DVD players complied with the DVD standard, they
inherently and unavoidably infringed the patent. They sought damages
based on their standard global FRAND royalty rates.

B. Arguments for the Defendant (Rajesh Bansal)
The defendants argued that Philips failed to physically reverse-engineer
their specific DVD players to prove infringement. They argued that
relying on theoretical "standards" is insufficient for a patent
infringement trial. Furthermore, they challenged the validity of the
patent and claimed the requested royalties were excessive and non-FRAND.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Philips, delivering India's first
post-trial final judgment declaring an SEP valid and infringed, and
awarding actual and punitive damages.
cases.reasoning:
This judgment cemented SEP jurisprudence in India. The Court accepted the
"Essentiality Mapping" methodology. The Court held that a plaintiff does
not need to reverse-engineer every single infringing device. If the
plaintiff proves that their patent claims map directly onto an industry
standard, and the defendant's device complies with that standard (as
evidenced by the DVD logo on the player), infringement is legally
established. Regarding damages, the Court validated Philips' FRAND
royalty rate, noting it was the same rate charged to hundreds of other
licensees globally. The Court calculated the total number of un-licensed
DVD players imported by the defendant and ordered them to pay the
standard royalty rate for every single unit, plus punitive damages for
years of unauthorized use.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Proof of SEP Infringement: In standard essential patent trials, proving
that the patent claims map exactly onto the mandatory industry standard,
and that the defendant's product complies with that standard, is
sufficient to prove infringement.

cases.title: N.D. TV v. ICC Development (International) Ltd.
cases.facts:
ICC Development held the exclusive broadcasting and copyright for ICC
cricket matches. They granted exclusive broadcast rights to ESPN Star
Sports. N.D. TV (a news channel) aired brief clips of the cricket matches
during their regular news bulletins. However, N.D. TV also created
specialized, 30-minute analytical cricket shows heavily utilizing the
match footage. These special shows were highly lucrative and brought in
specific corporate sponsors. ICC sued N.D. TV for copyright infringement.
N.D. TV relied on the defense of "Fair Dealing" under Section 52(1)(a) of
the Copyright Act for the purpose of "reporting current events."
cases.issues:
What are the boundaries of "fair dealing" when news channels use
copyrighted sports footage to report current events?

Does the creation of commercially sponsored, specialized programming
using copyrighted footage cross the line from news reporting to
commercial exploitation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Respondent (ICC)
ICC acknowledged that news channels have a right to show brief clips (a
few seconds) to report the match results. However, they argued that N.D.
TV's special 30-minute programs were not "news bulletins." They were
commercial entertainment shows designed to monetize the ICC's expensive
copyrighted footage without paying a licensing fee, directly damaging the
exclusive rights sold to ESPN.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Appellant (N.D. TV)
N.D. TV argued that cricket is a religion in India. Analyzing a match,
showing replays, and discussing player performance constitutes "reporting
current events." They argued that the public has a right to information,
and restricting news channels from using footage stifles journalistic
freedom.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court (Division Bench) ruled partially in favor of both.
They allowed brief clips for regular news but granted an injunction
strictly restricting the use of footage in sponsored, specialized
programming.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on the limits of Fair Dealing. The
Court held that the purpose of Section 52 is to protect the public's
right to news. Therefore, showing brief clips of a match in a standard,
general news bulletin is perfectly legal fair dealing. However, the Court
drew a strict red line at commercial exploitation. When a news channel
creates a special, half-hour show dedicated entirely to the cricket
match, loops the copyrighted footage, brings in experts to analyze it,
and most importantly, sells dedicated advertising space for that specific
show, it ceases to be mere "news reporting." It transforms into
commercial entertainment. Using another party's expensive intellectual
property as the foundation for a sponsored television show is not "fair,"
and therefore constitutes copyright infringement.
cases.legalPrinciples:
Limits of News Reporting Fair Dealing: While news organizations can use
short snippets of copyrighted sports broadcasts for general news
bulletins, creating specialized, commercially sponsored programming that
heavily relies on that footage exceeds the scope of fair dealing and
requires a copyright license.
